rd-school-c12-maths-b.ch08-application-i.title: Application of Integrals — Part 2: Areas Worked from Sketch to Answer
rd-school-c12-maths-b.ch08-application-i.subtitle: Lines, parabolas, circles and ellipses — every exercise type with the sketch that makes it easy

sections.h: Why the sketch is half the marks
sections.md:
Part 1 introduced the idea that a definite integral adds up thin strips, and showed vertical strips, horizontal strips, circles, ellipses, parabolas and lines, ending with a checklist.

This part walks through **every type of question** in the chapter. The habit to build is simple: **sketch first, integrate second**. A rough sketch tells you

- which variable to integrate in (vertical strips dx or horizontal strips dy),
- the limits (where curves cross axes or each other),
- whether any part lies below the axis (where the integral would come out negative), and
- whether symmetry lets you compute one piece and multiply.

We go in the chapter's order: area bounded by a curve and an axis between two lines; areas inside circles and ellipses; areas cut off by lines; and (for enrichment) regions between two curves.

> **Did you know?** Archimedes found the area of a parabolic segment around 250 BCE — it is exactly 4/3 of the inscribed triangle — by slicing it into ever-smaller triangles. That is integration, nearly 2,000 years before calculus had a name.

sections.h: The two strip rules, stated precisely
sections.md:
**Vertical strips.** For a curve y = f(x) ≥ 0 between x = a and x = b, a strip of width dx and height y has area y dx, so

**A = ∫ₐᵇ y dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.**

**Horizontal strips.** For x = g(y) ≥ 0 between y = c and y = d, the strip has length x and thickness dy:

**A = ∫ᶜᵈ x dy = ∫ᶜᵈ g(y) dy.**

**Below the axis.** If f(x) ≤ 0 on [a, b], the integral is negative; area = |∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx|.

**Crossing the axis.** If the curve is above on [a, c] and below on [c, b], **split**: A = ∫ₐᶜ f dx + |∫ᶜᵇ f dx|. Integrating straight through would let positive and negative parts cancel.

*Example.* Area between y = cos x and the x-axis for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. cos x is positive on [0, π/2], negative on [π/2, 3π/2], positive on [3π/2, 2π]. Areas: 1 + 2 + 1 = **4 square units**. Integrating straight through gives sin 2π − sin 0 = 0 — clearly wrong for an area.

*Example.* Area bounded by y = x³, the x-axis and x = −2, x = 1: |∫₋₂⁰ x³ dx| + ∫₀¹ x³ dx = |−4| + ¼ = 17/4.

fig.caption: y = cos x on [0, 2π]: the part below the axis must be counted with a plus sign.
fig.alt: Cosine curve with green areas above and a pulsing red area below the axis.

check.q: The area between y = sin x and the x-axis for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π is:
check.why: Each half wave has area 2 (∫₀^π sin x dx = 2), and both halves count positively.

sections.md:
**Area of y² = 9x between x = 2 and x = 4 (first quadrant).** y = 3√x, so A = ∫₂⁴ 3x^(1/2) dx = 2[x^(3/2)]₂⁴ = 2(8 − 2√2) = 16 − 4√2.

**Area bounded by y² = 4x, the x-axis... and the line x = 3 (both quadrants).** By symmetry about the x-axis: A = 2∫₀³ 2√x dx = 4 · (2/3)(3^(3/2)) = (8/3)(3√3) = 8√3.

**Area of x² = 4y with y = 2, y = 4 and the y-axis (first quadrant).** Use horizontal strips: x = 2√y, A = ∫₂⁴ 2√y dy = (4/3)[y^(3/2)]₂⁴ = (4/3)(8 − 2√2) = (32 − 8√2)/3.

**Area cut off by the latus rectum.** For y² = 4ax, the latus rectum is the line x = a. A = 2∫₀ᵃ 2√(ax) dx = 4√a · (2/3)a^(3/2) = **(8/3)a²**. For y² = 12x (a = 3): 24 square units.

**Parabola and a horizontal line: y = x² and y = 4.** Horizontal strips: x = √y, region symmetric about the y-axis: A = 2∫₀⁴ √y dy = 2 · (2/3) · 8 = 32/3. (Check with vertical strips: ∫₋₂² (4 − x²) dx = 16 − 16/3 = 32/3 ✓.)

**Line through a parabola.** Area between y = x² and y = x: they meet at x = 0 and 1, line on top: ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = ½ − ⅓ = **1/6**.

fig.alt: Sideways parabola with shaded region up to a dashed vertical line and a moving strip.

sections.h: Circles: from a quarter to a segment
sections.md:
**Whole circle x² + y² = a².** First quadrant: y = √(a² − x²), A₁ = ∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx = [(x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a)]₀ᵃ = (a²/2)(π/2) = πa²/4. Four quadrants: **πa²** — the formula you knew, now proved.

**Circle x² + y² = 16 in the first quadrant** is therefore 4π.

**Area between the circle x² + y² = 4 and the line x = 1 (the smaller segment, right side).** A = 2∫₁² √(4 − x²) dx = 2[(x/2)√(4 − x²) + 2 sin⁻¹(x/2)]₁² = 2[(0 + 2 · π/2) − (½√3 + 2 · π/6)] = 2[π − √3/2 − π/3] = 2[2π/3 − √3/2] = **4π/3 − √3**.

**First-quadrant area between x² + y² = 32, the line y = x and the x-axis.** They meet at (4, 4). From 0 to 4 the region lies under the line; from 4 to √32 under the circle:
A = ∫₀⁴ x dx + ∫₄^(4√2) √(32 − x²) dx = 8 + [(x/2)√(32 − x²) + 16 sin⁻¹(x/(4√2))]₄^(4√2) = 8 + [16 · π/2 − (8 + 16 · π/4)] = 8 + 8π − 8 − 4π = **4π**. (Sanity check: the region is an eighth of the circle, π · 32/8 = 4π ✓.)

check.q: The area of the circle x² + y² = 9 in the first quadrant is:
check.why: A quarter of πr² with r = 3 is 9π/4.

sections.md:
**x²/a² + y²/b² = 1.** First quadrant: y = (b/a)√(a² − x²), so A₁ = (b/a) · πa²/4 = πab/4, and the whole ellipse is **πab**. When a = b this becomes πa², the circle — a good check.

*Example.* x²/16 + y²/9 = 1: area = π · 4 · 3 = 12π.

*Example.* 4x² + 9y² = 36, i.e. x²/9 + y²/4 = 1: area 6π.

**Ellipse and a chord.** The smaller region cut off from x²/9 + y²/4 = 1 by the line x/3 + y/2 = 1 (joining (3, 0) and (0, 2)). In the first quadrant, area under the ellipse = πab/4 = 3π/2. Area under the line = triangle ½ · 3 · 2 = 3. Required area = **3π/2 − 3 = (3/2)(π − 2)**.

Similarly, for x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 and x/a + y/b = 1, the small segment is (ab/4)(π − 2).

**Why ellipses matter.** Planetary orbits are ellipses (Kepler's first law), and Kepler's second law says the line from the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times — so area under an elliptical arc is a real astronomical tool. Engineers also use πab for elliptical manholes, pipes and the cross-section of an egg-shaped sewer.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='280' fill='#f3f9f1'/><line x1='60' y1='140' x2='540' y2='140' stroke='#888'/><line x1='300' y1='20' x2='300' y2='260' stroke='#888'/><ellipse cx='300' cy='140' rx='210' ry='100' fill='none' stroke='#2e7d32' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M510,140 A210,100 0 0 0 300,40 Z' fill='#a5d6a7' fill-opacity='.7'/><polygon points='300,140 510,140 300,40' fill='#fff59d' fill-opacity='.9'/><circle r='6' fill='#e65100'><animateMotion dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite' path='M510,140 A210,100 0 1 0 90,140 A210,100 0 1 0 510,140'/></circle><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' fill='#222'><text x='420' y='60'>segment = πab/4 − ab/2</text><text x='310' y='130'>triangle</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Quarter ellipse minus the triangle under the chord leaves the curved segment (ab/4)(π − 2).
fig.alt: Ellipse with a quarter shaded, a triangle inside it, and a dot orbiting.

check.q: The area of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/16 = 1 is:
check.why: Area = πab = π × 5 × 4 = 20π.

sections.md:
A region bounded only by straight lines can always be found by coordinate geometry, but the exercises ask you to do it by integration — good practice for setting up limits.

*Line y = 3x + 2, the x-axis and x = −1, x = 1.* The line crosses the axis at x = −2/3. Below the axis on [−1, −2/3]: |∫₋₁^(−2/3) (3x + 2) dx| = |[3x²/2 + 2x]| = |(2/3 − 4/3) − (3/2 − 2)| = |−2/3 + 1/2| = 1/6. Above on [−2/3, 1]: [3x²/2 + 2x] from −2/3 to 1 = (3/2 + 2) − (−2/3) = 7/2 + 2/3 = 25/6. Total **26/6 = 13/3**.

*Triangle with vertices (1, 0), (2, 2), (3, 1).* Lines: AB: y = 2(x − 1); BC: y = −x + 4; AC: y = (x − 1)/2. Area = ∫₁² [2(x − 1) − (x − 1)/2] dx + ∫₂³ [(4 − x) − (x − 1)/2] dx = ∫₁² (3/2)(x − 1) dx + ∫₂³ (9/2 − 3x/2) dx = 3/4 + [9x/2 − 3x²/4]₂³ = 3/4 + (27/2 − 27/4) − (9 − 3) = 3/4 + 27/4 − 6 = **3/2**. Check by the determinant formula from Chapter 4: ½|1(2 − 1) + 2(1 − 0) + 3(0 − 2)| = ½|1 + 2 − 6| = 3/2 ✓.

**Linking chapters:** integration and determinants agree, as they must. Examiners like asking for one method and checking with the other.

check.q: The area bounded by y = x, the x-axis and x = 2 is:
check.why: ∫₀² x dx = 2, the triangle with base 2 and height 2.

sections.h: Going further: area between two curves
sections.md:
If f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b], the area between them is **∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx** — top minus bottom, whatever their positions relative to the axis. With horizontal strips: right minus left, ∫[x_R − x_L] dy.

**Steps:** (1) solve the equations together to get intersection points; (2) decide which is on top in each interval; (3) integrate the difference, splitting where they swap.

*Two parabolas y² = 4x and x² = 4y.* They meet at (0, 0) and (4, 4). On [0, 4], √(4x) = 2√x is above x²/4. A = ∫₀⁴ (2√x − x²/4) dx = (4/3)(8) − 64/12 = 32/3 − 16/3 = **16/3**.

*Circle and parabola.* The region inside x² + y² = 4... these problems combine √ forms from Chapter 7 with parabola integrals; always use symmetry and sketch.

This topic is a natural extension and appears in many entrance exams even where a board syllabus trims it, so it is worth knowing.

**Final exam checklist**
1. Sketch with intercepts and intersections labelled.
2. Shade the region — say in words what it is.
3. Choose strips; write limits.
4. Use symmetry.
5. Split at axis crossings.
6. Use the √(a² − x²) form for circles and ellipses.
7. Units: 'square units'.
8. Sanity check against a known shape (triangle, quarter circle).

Vertical strips: A = ∫ y dx; horizontal: A = ∫ x dy.
Parts below the axis must be taken with modulus; split at crossings.

Area of circle πa² and of ellipse πab follow from ∫√(a² − x²) dx.
Ellipse segment cut by x/a + y/b = 1 is (ab/4)(π − 2).
Regions bounded by lines can be checked with the determinant formula.
Between two curves: ∫(top − bottom) dx over the intersection interval.
Always state answers in square units.

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch03-current-ele.title: Current Electricity
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch03-current-ele.subtitle: Why a switch lights the bulb instantly even though electrons crawl slower than an ant

sections.h: 1. The mystery of the slow electrons
sections.md:
Flip the switch in your room in Pune and the tube light glows at once. Yet, as you will calculate in this chapter, the electrons in the copper wire drift at roughly **a tenth of a millimetre per second** — slower than a snail. How can a crawl produce an instant result?

The answer is that the wire is already *full* of free electrons. When you close the switch, an electric field spreads along the wire at nearly the speed of light, and every free electron everywhere in the circuit starts drifting at almost the same moment. It is like a pipe already full of water: push at one end and water comes out of the other end immediately.

In Chapter 1 and 2 you studied charges at rest (electrostatics). Now charges **move**, and we ask: what makes them move, what resists them, how much energy do they carry, and how do we analyse networks of resistors and cells? By the end you should be able to solve any DC circuit in the NCERT style using Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's rules and the Wheatstone bridge.

**Electric current** is the rate of flow of charge through a cross-section:

I = q / t  (steady current), or I = dq/dt in general.

The SI unit is the **ampere (A)**: one coulomb per second. Typical values: a mobile charger supplies about 1–3 A, a household geyser draws about 10 A, a lightning stroke carries tens of thousands of amperes for a fraction of a second, and nerve signals involve microamperes.

By convention, the direction of current is the direction in which *positive* charge would flow — opposite to the actual motion of electrons in a metal. Current is a scalar (it obeys ordinary addition at junctions, not vector addition), even though we draw arrows to show its sense.

> **Did you know?** Even in a wire carrying no current, free electrons zip around at about 10⁵–10⁶ m/s due to thermal motion. They just go in random directions, so the net flow is zero.
keyTerms: Electric current — rate of flow of charge, I = dq/dt
Ampere — 1 C of charge per second
Conventional current — direction of flow of positive charge

check.q: A charge of 120 C flows through a wire in 1 minute. The current is:
check.why: Current is charge divided by time, so 120 C / 60 s = 2 A.

sections.h: 2. Drift velocity, mobility and the origin of resistance
sections.md:
Picture the free electrons in copper as a crowd in a busy Mumbai local station. With no field, everyone moves randomly; the *average* velocity is zero. Switch on a field **E** and each electron feels a force −eE, so between collisions it accelerates by a = −eE/m. Every collision with a vibrating ion scrambles its direction again.

If the average time between collisions (the **relaxation time**) is τ, the average velocity picked up is the **drift velocity**:

v_d = −(eE/m) τ

Now count how much charge crosses an area A in time Δt. Electrons within a length v_dΔt of the area cross it; there are n·A·v_dΔt of them (n = number density of free electrons). So

I = n e A v_d

Combining the two: I = (n e² τ / m) A E. Define **current density** j = I/A, and we get j = σE, with conductivity

σ = n e² τ / m,  and resistivity ρ = 1/σ = m / (n e² τ).

This is the microscopic form of Ohm's law. It tells us resistivity depends on **n** (how many carriers) and **τ** (how often they collide).

**Mobility** μ is drift speed per unit field: μ = v_d / E = eτ/m. Unit: m²/(V·s). Semiconductors with high electron mobility make faster chips.

**Typical numbers.** For copper, n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. A 1.5 A current in a wire of cross-section 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² gives v_d = I/(neA) = 1.5 / (8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻³ m/s — about one millimetre per second.

Drift velocity — average velocity of electrons due to the field
Mobility — drift velocity per unit electric field

check.q: If the relaxation time of electrons in a metal doubles (all else fixed), its resistivity:
check.why: Resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ) is inversely proportional to τ, so doubling τ halves ρ.

sections.md:
Georg Simon Ohm found that for many conductors at constant temperature, the current is proportional to the potential difference: **V = IR**. The constant R is the **resistance**, measured in ohms (Ω).

Resistance depends on the shape of the conductor. Double the length and electrons must push through twice as many ions: R doubles. Double the cross-sectional area and twice as many lanes open: R halves. So

R = ρ L / A

where **ρ (resistivity)** is a property of the material alone (unit Ω·m). Rough values at room temperature:

| Material | ρ (Ω·m) | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Silver | 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ | conductor |
| Copper | 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ | conductor |
| Nichrome | ~1.0 × 10⁻⁶ | alloy (heaters) |
| Germanium | ~0.46 | semiconductor |
| Glass | 10¹⁰ – 10¹⁴ | insulator |

Nichrome sits in your electric iron because its resistivity is high and changes little with temperature. Copper is for wiring because it wastes little energy.

**Limitations of Ohm's law.** Ohm's law is not a universal law of nature; it is a property of *ohmic* materials. Non-ohmic behaviour includes:
- V–I graph not a straight line (e.g., a filament lamp heats up).
- Current depends on the direction of V (a diode).
- The same V gives more than one I (e.g., GaAs shows a region of negative resistance).

**Colour code.** Carbon resistors carry coloured bands: Black 0, Brown 1, Red 2, Orange 3, Yellow 4, Green 5, Blue 6, Violet 7, Grey 8, White 9. The first two bands are digits, the third is the multiplier (power of 10), and the fourth is tolerance (gold ±5%, silver ±10%, none ±20%). A mnemonic many students use: *B B ROY of Great Britain has a Very Good Wife*.

check.q: A wire of resistance R is stretched to twice its length (volume constant). New resistance is:
check.why: Doubling length at constant volume halves the area, so R = ρL/A becomes ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4R.

sections.md:
Heat a metal and its ions vibrate more violently, so electrons collide more often: τ falls and ρ rises. Over a moderate range,

ρ_T = ρ₀ [1 + α (T − T₀)]

where α is the **temperature coefficient of resistivity**. For copper α ≈ 4 × 10⁻³ per °C. Alloys like manganin and constantan have tiny α, which is why they are used for standard resistors in labs.

In **semiconductors** the story is reversed. Heating frees more charge carriers, so n rises steeply, overwhelming the drop in τ. Resistivity *decreases* with temperature — α is negative. Thermistors in your refrigerator and in digital thermometers use this effect.

At very low temperatures some materials become **superconductors** with exactly zero resistance — the basis of MRI magnets.

> **Did you know?** A 100 W filament bulb has a cold resistance roughly ten times lower than its hot resistance, so it draws a big surge of current at the instant of switching on. That is why old bulbs usually fused just as you switched them on.

check.q: The resistance of a semiconductor sample as temperature rises:
check.why: More carriers are released by heat, so n rises sharply and resistivity falls.

sections.md:
When charge Q moves through a potential drop V, it loses energy QV. In a resistor this energy turns into heat (collisions with ions). The rate is power:

P = V I = I² R = V² / R

This is **Joule heating**. It's useful in heaters, irons, toasters and fuses, and wasteful in transmission lines.

**Why power lines use high voltage.** A power station sends power P through cables of resistance R_c. The current needed is I = P/V, and the loss in the cables is I² R_c = P² R_c / V². Raising V by a factor of 10 cuts losses by a factor of 100. That's why India's grid transmits at 220 kV, 400 kV and even 765 kV, then steps down to 230 V for homes using transformers (Chapter 7).

**Electricity bill units.** One 'unit' on your MSEDCL or BESCOM bill is 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. A 1.5 kW AC running 8 hours a day uses 12 units a day. At ₹7 per unit that's ₹84 per day.
keyTerms: Joule heating — conversion of electrical energy into heat in a resistor
kWh — commercial unit of energy = 3.6 MJ

check.q: Two bulbs of 60 W and 100 W rated for 220 V are connected in series to 220 V. Which glows brighter?
check.why: The 60 W bulb has higher resistance (R = V²/P), and in series the same current flows, so P = I²R is larger for the 60 W bulb.

sections.md:
**Series:** the same current passes through each resistor; voltages add.

R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + …

**Parallel:** the same voltage is across each; currents add.

1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + …

For two in parallel, R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂). The parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest resistor — that's why adding more appliances at home increases the total current drawn.

Household wiring is parallel: each appliance gets full 230 V and can be switched independently. Decorative serial lights for Diwali are often in series — one dead bulb (in older sets) darkens the whole string.

Solving a ladder: start at the far end and collapse pairs step by step, redrawing the circuit after each step. Symmetry helps: points at equal potential can be joined or separated without changing anything.

sections.md:
A cell uses chemical energy to push charge from its negative to its positive terminal *inside* the cell. The work done per unit charge is the **emf ε** (electromotive force — it's actually an energy per charge, not a force).

Real cells have **internal resistance r** due to the electrolyte. When the cell supplies current I to an external resistor R:

I = ε / (R + r),  terminal voltage V = ε − I r

So the terminal voltage drops as you draw more current. When I = 0 (open circuit), V = ε. When charging a cell, current enters the + terminal and V = ε + Ir.

That's why a weak car battery may show 12 V on a voltmeter yet fail to crank the engine: its internal resistance has risen, so at the large starting current the terminal voltage collapses.

**Cells in series:** emfs add (with signs) and internal resistances add: ε_eq = ε₁ + ε₂, r_eq = r₁ + r₂.

**Cells in parallel:** ε_eq = (ε₁ r₂ + ε₂ r₁)/(r₁ + r₂), and 1/r_eq = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂.

For n identical cells in series: nε and nr. In parallel: ε and r/n.

sections.md:
Series–parallel tricks fail for circuits with several cells in different branches. Gustav Kirchhoff gave two rules that solve *any* DC network.

**Junction rule (KCL):** at any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum leaving. This is conservation of charge — charge doesn't pile up in a steady state.

**Loop rule (KVL):** around any closed loop, the algebraic sum of potential changes is zero. This is conservation of energy — come back to the same point, and you have the same potential.

**Sign convention (stick to one!):**
- Going through a resistor *in the direction* of the assumed current: −IR. Against it: +IR.
- Going through a cell from − to +: +ε. From + to −: −ε.

**Method:**
1. Assign a current to every branch with an arbitrary direction; use KCL to reduce unknowns.
2. Write KVL for enough independent loops.
3. Solve. A negative answer simply means the actual direction is opposite to your guess.

Kirchhoff's rules power circuit simulators like SPICE, which engineers in Bengaluru's chip-design firms run millions of times a day.

check.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a consequence of conservation of:
check.why: In a steady state charge cannot accumulate at a junction, so what flows in must flow out.

sections.h: 9. The Wheatstone bridge and the metre bridge
sections.md:
Four resistors P, Q, R, S form a diamond. A cell is connected across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. Adjust until the galvanometer shows zero: the bridge is **balanced** and

P / Q = R / S

Proof sketch: with zero galvanometer current, the current I₁ through P also flows through Q, and I₂ through R also through S. The two galvanometer ends are at equal potential, so I₁P = I₂R and I₁Q = I₂S. Divide to get P/Q = R/S.

Because the result is a null reading, it doesn't depend on the galvanometer's resistance or the cell's emf — a very precise method.

**Metre bridge.** A practical form: a 1 m uniform wire stretched on a board, a known resistance R in one gap and an unknown S in the other. A jockey slides along the wire until the galvanometer reads zero at length l from one end. Since wire resistance is proportional to length,

R / S = l / (100 − l)  (l in cm), so S = R (100 − l)/l.

Tip from your lab: choose R so that the balance point lies near the middle (40–60 cm) to reduce end errors.

*(Note: the current NCERT syllabus has dropped the potentiometer from this chapter; some state boards still teach it. The principle is the same — balancing potential drops along a uniform wire.)*

parts.md: During a power cut in Nagpur, Meera's grandfather handed her an old torch with two cells. It glowed bright for a second, then faded to an orange smear. 'The cells are new,' he grumbled, 'I bought them from Sharma uncle's shop yesterday.' Meera took out her school multimeter. Across each cell, with nothing connected: 1.5 V. Perfect. Then she switched on the torch and measured again: 1.1 V across each. Where had the missing 0.4 V gone?

She remembered her chapter: V = ε − Ir. The bulb drew about 0.4 A. So 0.4 = 0.4 × r, giving r ≈ 1 Ω for each cell — high for a fresh cell. She checked the date on the packet: two years old. The electrolyte had partly dried, raising internal resistance. The emf was still 1.5 V, but the cells could no longer deliver current without wasting most of the push inside themselves. Grandfather laughed: 'So the shop sold me tired cells that look healthy when nobody asks them to work.' Exactly, said Meera — an open-circuit voltmeter reading is no proof of a cell's health.

summary: Current I = dq/dt; SI unit ampere; conventional direction is that of positive charge.
Drift velocity v_d = eEτ/m; I = neAv_d; drift speeds are ~mm/s or less.
Microscopic Ohm's law: j = σE with σ = ne²τ/m.
Mobility μ = v_d/E = eτ/m.
R = ρL/A; ρ is a material property; stretching a wire n times multiplies R by n².
Metals: ρ rises with T (α > 0); semiconductors: ρ falls with T.
Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
Series: R adds; parallel: reciprocals add.
Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir while discharging, ε + Ir while charging.
Kirchhoff's junction rule = charge conservation; loop rule = energy conservation.
Balanced Wheatstone bridge: P/Q = R/S; metre bridge S = R(100 − l)/l.
Ohm's law fails for diodes, filaments at changing temperature and materials like GaAs.

glossary.d: Work done by a source per unit charge in moving charge through it
Resistance of the material inside a cell
A measurement made when a detector reads zero
Reciprocal of resistivity, σ = 1/ρ

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch03-current-ele.title: Current Electricity — Part 2: The Numerical Workshop
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch03-current-ele.subtitle: Drift speeds, colour codes, cell combinations, Kirchhoff loops and the metre bridge — solved step by step

sections.md:
Part 1 told the whole story of the chapter — drift velocity and mobility, Ohm's law and resistivity, temperature dependence, energy and power, combinations of resistors, emf and internal resistance, Kirchhoff's rules and the Wheatstone and metre bridges.

Part 2 is for doing. Each section takes one exercise type from the chapter, gives the formula sheet in a line, and works a typical problem with Indian-household numbers. Keep a calculator and a pencil ready and try each one before reading the steps.

> **Did you know?** A household copper wire carries a few amperes, yet the electrons inside drift at well under a millimetre per second. The lamp lights almost instantly because the electric field travels through the wire at close to the speed of light, pushing all the electrons at once — like water already filling a pipe.

**Formulas:** I = neAv_d, j = I/A = nev_d, v_d = eEτ/m, mobility μ = v_d/E = eτ/m, resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ).

*Problem.* A copper wire of cross-section 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² carries 1.5 A. Free-electron density n = 9.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Find v_d.

v_d = I/(neA) = 1.5/(9.0 × 10²⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 1.5/(1.44 × 10³) ≈ **1.04 × 10⁻³ m/s**, about 1 mm/s.

*Compare* with thermal speeds of about 10⁵ m/s: the drift is a tiny bias on a furious random motion.

*Relaxation time from resistivity.* For copper ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m: τ = m/(ne²ρ) = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹/(9.0 × 10²⁸ × 2.56 × 10⁻³⁸ × 1.7 × 10⁻⁸) ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁴ s.

check.q: If the current in a wire is doubled, the drift velocity:
check.why: v_d = I/(neA), so for the same wire it is directly proportional to the current.

sections.md:
**R = ρl/A.** Stretching a wire to n times its length (volume constant) multiplies its resistance by **n²**, because the length goes up n times and the area goes down n times.

*Problem.* A 10 Ω wire is stretched to twice its length. New R = 40 Ω.

**Carbon resistor colour code** (Black 0, Brown 1, Red 2, Orange 3, Yellow 4, Green 5, Blue 6, Violet 7, Grey 8, White 9; tolerance gold 5 %, silver 10 %). A resistor banded yellow–violet–red–gold is 47 × 10² Ω = **4.7 kΩ ± 5 %**.

**Temperature.** ρ_T = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]. Metals have α > 0, semiconductors α < 0; alloys like nichrome and manganin have very small α, which is why they are used in heaters and standard resistors.

*Problem.* A heater's nichrome element has 75.3 Ω at 27 °C. With 230 V it settles at 2.68 A. α = 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. Find its steady temperature.
R_T = 230/2.68 = 85.8 Ω. 85.8 = 75.3[1 + 1.70 × 10⁻⁴ (T − 27)] ⇒ T − 27 = (85.8/75.3 − 1)/(1.70 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.1394/1.70 × 10⁴ ≈ 820 ⇒ **T ≈ 847 °C**.

sections.h: Power, energy and the electricity bill
sections.md:
**P = VI = I²R = V²/R.** 1 kWh ('one unit') = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

*Problem.* A 1500 W geyser runs 40 minutes a day for 30 days at ₹7 per unit. Energy = 1.5 kW × (2/3) h × 30 = 30 kWh. Cost = **₹210**.

*Problem.* Two bulbs, 100 W and 60 W (both rated 220 V), are joined in **series** across 220 V. Which glows brighter? R = V²/P: 484 Ω and 806.7 Ω. In series the current is the same, so P = I²R is larger for the larger R: the **60 W bulb glows brighter**. In parallel the 100 W bulb is brighter. A classic exam trap.

**Power transmission.** Loss in lines = I²R_c. For the same power P = VI, raising the voltage lowers I, so power stations transmit at very high voltage (hundreds of kV) and step it down near homes.

check.q: A 100 W and a 60 W bulb (same rated voltage) in series: which is brighter?
check.why: In series both carry the same current, and the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance, so I²R is greater for it.

sections.h: Cells: emf, terminal voltage and combinations
sections.md:
**Single cell:** V = ε − Ir while discharging; I = ε/(R + r).

**Series (n identical):** ε_eq = nε, r_eq = nr. **Two different cells in series:** ε_eq = ε₁ + ε₂, r_eq = r₁ + r₂ (if one is reversed, subtract the emfs).

**Parallel:** ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂), 1/r_eq = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂. For n identical cells: ε_eq = ε, r_eq = r/n.

*Problem.* A 12 V battery with r = 0.4 Ω is charged... let us discharge it instead through 5.6 Ω: I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A, terminal V = 12 − 0.8 = **11.2 V**.

*Problem (charging).* A 8.0 V battery with r = 0.5 Ω is charged from a 120 V supply through a 15.5 Ω series resistor. I = (120 − 8)/(15.5 + 0.5) = 112/16 = 7.0 A. Terminal voltage during charging = ε + Ir = 8 + 3.5 = **11.5 V** — higher than the emf, because current flows into the cell.

*Problem (parallel).* Cells 2 V, 1 Ω and 3 V, 2 Ω in parallel: ε_eq = (2·2 + 3·1)/3 = 7/3 V ≈ 2.33 V; r_eq = 2/3 Ω.

check.q: While a cell is being charged, its terminal voltage is:
check.why: Current is forced into the cell, so V = ε + Ir exceeds the emf.

sections.h: Kirchhoff's rules on a two-loop circuit
sections.md:
**Junction rule** (charge conservation): currents in = currents out. **Loop rule** (energy conservation): Σ(emf) = Σ(IR) round any closed loop, with signs taken consistently.

*Problem.* A 10 V cell (negligible r) in the left branch, a 6 V cell in the right branch, both positive terminals at the top, joined by a common middle branch of 4 Ω. Left branch resistance 2 Ω, right 2 Ω. Find the current in each branch.

Let I₁ flow up the left branch, I₂ up the right branch, and both come down through the middle: I₃ = I₁ + I₂.
Left loop: 10 = 2I₁ + 4(I₁ + I₂) ⇒ 6I₁ + 4I₂ = 10.
Right loop: 6 = 2I₂ + 4(I₁ + I₂) ⇒ 4I₁ + 6I₂ = 6.
Solve: multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: 18I₁ + 12I₂ = 30, 8I₁ + 12I₂ = 12 ⇒ 10I₁ = 18 ⇒ **I₁ = 1.8 A**. Then 4I₂ = 10 − 10.8 ⇒ **I₂ = −0.2 A** (it actually flows down the right branch — the 10 V cell is charging the 6 V one). Middle: **I₃ = 1.6 A**. Check right loop: 2(−0.2) + 4(1.6) = −0.4 + 6.4 = 6 ✓.

A negative answer is never an error in Kirchhoff problems — it just means your guessed direction was backwards.

check.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule is a statement of conservation of:
check.why: Round a closed loop the net work done per unit charge must be zero, which is energy conservation.

sections.md:
**Balance condition:** P/Q = R/S, galvanometer current zero.

*Check balance.* P = 10, Q = 20, R = 15, S = 30 Ω: 10/20 = 15/30 ✓ balanced; the galvanometer branch can be removed.

**Metre bridge:** with balance at length l cm from the end next to the known R: **S = R(100 − l)/l** (unknown S in the right gap).

*Problem.* Balance at 39.5 cm with R = 12.5 Ω in the left gap: S = 12.5 × 60.5/39.5 ≈ **19.1 Ω**.

*Problem.* Interchange the resistors; the new balance point is at 100 − 39.5 = **60.5 cm**. If a different reading appears, the bridge has end errors.

*Why balance near the middle?* Percentage error is smallest when l ≈ 50 cm, since a reading error of ±0.1 cm matters less relative to both l and (100 − l).

> **Did you know?** The bridge is named after Charles Wheatstone, who popularised it in 1843, though Samuel Christie had described it ten years earlier.

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch04-moving-char.title: Moving Charges and Magnetism
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch04-moving-char.subtitle: How a twitching compass needle in 1820 unified electricity and magnetism

sections.md:
In 1820, Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a compass needle near a current-carrying wire swung round. Switch the current off, and it returned to north. Reverse the current, and it swung the other way. Electricity — moving charge — makes magnetism.

This chapter follows that thread: moving charges create magnetic fields, and magnetic fields push on moving charges. From these two facts we get cyclotrons, MRI scanners, electric motors and the galvanometer in your school lab.

The **magnetic field B** is a vector field. Its SI unit is the **tesla (T)**. The Earth's field is about 3 × 10⁻⁵ to 5 × 10⁻⁵ T; a fridge magnet about 10⁻² T; an MRI magnet 1.5–3 T. An older unit, the gauss, equals 10⁻⁴ T.

We draw B with field lines and use the convention: ⊙ means field out of the page (the tip of an arrow coming at you), ⊗ means into the page (the tail feathers).

check.q: The SI unit of magnetic field is:
check.why: B is measured in tesla; 1 T = 1 N/(A·m), and 1 gauss is 10⁻⁴ T.

sections.md:
A charge q moving with velocity **v** in electric field **E** and magnetic field **B** feels

**F = q(E + v × B)**

The magnetic part, F = q v B sin θ, has striking properties:
- It is zero if the charge is at rest or moves parallel to B.
- It is perpendicular to both v and B (use the right-hand rule: fingers along v, curl toward B, thumb gives F for a positive charge).
- Because it is always perpendicular to velocity, it **does no work**. It changes the direction of motion, never the speed or kinetic energy.

This definition also defines the tesla: a 1 C charge moving at 1 m/s perpendicular to a 1 T field feels 1 N.

**Force on a current-carrying conductor.** A wire of length l carries current I in field B. Summing forces on all drifting electrons gives

**F = I l × B**,  magnitude F = B I l sin θ.

This is the push that turns every motor — from a ceiling fan to a Vande Bharat traction motor.
keyTerms: Lorentz force — total force q(E + v×B) on a moving charge
Right-hand rule — finds direction of v×B

check.q: An electron enters a magnetic field parallel to the field lines. Its path is:
check.why: When v is parallel to B, sin θ = 0, so there is no magnetic force and the electron continues straight.

sections.h: 3. Circular and helical motion; velocity selector
sections.md:
If v is perpendicular to uniform B, the magnetic force provides centripetal force:

qvB = mv²/r  ⇒  r = mv/(qB)

The angular frequency ω = qB/m, and the frequency ν = qB/(2πm) — independent of speed! Faster particles make bigger circles in the same time. This **cyclotron frequency** is the key idea behind the cyclotron.

If v has a component along B too, the particle moves in a **helix**: circular motion with v⊥ and steady drift with v∥. The **pitch** (distance advanced per turn) is p = v∥ × T = 2π m v∥/(qB). Charged particles from the Sun spiral along Earth's field lines into polar regions, producing the aurora.

**Velocity selector.** Cross E and B at right angles. Electric force qE and magnetic force qvB oppose each other. Only particles with **v = E/B** pass undeflected. J. J. Thomson used this idea to measure e/m for the electron.

**Cyclotron.** Two hollow D-shaped electrodes ('dees') sit in a strong magnetic field with an oscillating voltage across the gap. An ion circles inside a dee, is accelerated each time it crosses the gap, and spirals outward with growing energy. Because the period doesn't depend on speed, a fixed-frequency oscillator keeps in step (the resonance condition ν_a = ν_c). India's Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre in Kolkata runs such machines for nuclear research and isotope production. Maximum kinetic energy: K = q²B²R²/(2m), with R the dee radius.

check.q: In a cyclotron, doubling the speed of a proton makes its time period:
check.why: T = 2πm/(qB) does not depend on speed, so the period is unchanged.

sections.h: 4. Biot–Savart law and the field of a circular loop
sections.md:
How much field does a tiny piece of current produce? The **Biot–Savart law** says a current element I dl at distance r gives

dB = (μ₀/4π) · I dl × r̂ / r²,  magnitude dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl sin θ / r²

where μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A is the permeability of free space. Compare Coulomb's law: both are inverse-square, but Biot–Savart has a sin θ and a direction perpendicular to both dl and r.

**Field on the axis of a circular loop** (radius R, current I, distance x from centre): by symmetry the perpendicular components cancel and the axial ones add:

B = μ₀ I R² / [2 (x² + R²)^(3/2)]

At the centre (x = 0): **B = μ₀ I / (2R)**. For N turns, multiply by N.

Direction: curl the fingers of your right hand along the current; the thumb points along B. Viewed from one face, a loop with anticlockwise current acts like a north pole facing you.

Also useful: the field of a **straight wire** of infinite length at distance r is B = μ₀I/(2πr), with circular field lines (right-hand thumb rule: thumb along current, fingers curl along B).

check.q: A circular coil of 100 turns, radius 10 cm, carries 1 A. B at the centre is about:

sections.h: 5. Ampere's circuital law, solenoids and toroids
sections.md:
For symmetric current distributions, there's a shortcut. **Ampere's circuital law**:

∮ B · dl = μ₀ I_enclosed

The line integral of B around any closed loop equals μ₀ times the net current threading the loop. It plays the role Gauss's law played in electrostatics.

**Long straight wire:** take a circle of radius r. B is constant and tangent, so B(2πr) = μ₀I, giving B = μ₀I/(2πr). Done in one line!

**Solenoid:** a long tightly wound coil with n turns per unit length. Inside, the field is uniform and along the axis; outside it is nearly zero. Taking a rectangular loop of length h: Bh = μ₀(nh)I, so

**B = μ₀ n I**

A solenoid is how we make a controllable uniform field — in relays, doorbells, MRI scanners and the electromagnets that lift scrap at a steel yard in Jamshedpur.

**Toroid:** a solenoid bent into a ring with N total turns. Inside the core, at radius r, B = μ₀NI/(2πr); in the open space inside and outside the ring, B = 0.

sections.h: 6. Force between parallel currents — defining the ampere
sections.md:
Wire a carries I_a and produces B = μ₀I_a/(2πd) at wire b, a distance d away. Wire b, with current I_b, feels a force per unit length

f = F/L = μ₀ I_a I_b / (2π d)

**Parallel currents attract; antiparallel currents repel** — the opposite of the rule for like charges!

This was historically used to define the ampere: two infinitely long parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, carrying equal currents, that exert 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre on each other carry 1 A each. (Since 2019 the SI defines the ampere by fixing the elementary charge e exactly, but the force law remains true and is a good exam point.)

check.q: Two parallel wires carry currents in opposite directions. They:
check.why: Antiparallel currents repel; parallel currents attract.

sections.h: 7. Torque on a current loop; the magnetic dipole
sections.md:
Put a rectangular loop (area A, N turns, current I) in uniform field B. Net force is zero, but the forces on opposite sides form a couple. The torque is

**τ = N I A B sin θ = m × B**

where **m = NIA** is the **magnetic dipole moment** (direction by the right-hand rule, perpendicular to the loop) and θ is the angle between m and B. Torque is maximum when the plane of the loop is parallel to B and zero when it is perpendicular.

So a current loop behaves exactly like a bar magnet. Even an electron orbiting a nucleus is a tiny current loop; its moment is quantised in units of the **Bohr magneton** μ_B = eh/(4πm_e) ≈ 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ A·m².

The orbiting electron's moment relates to its angular momentum: μ_l = (e/2m_e) L.

check.q: Torque on a current loop in a uniform field is maximum when the angle between m and B is:
check.why: τ = mB sin θ, which is largest when sin θ = 1, i.e. θ = 90°.

sections.h: 8. The moving-coil galvanometer, ammeter and voltmeter
sections.md:
A **moving-coil galvanometer** has a coil of N turns, area A, pivoted in a radial magnetic field made by concave pole pieces and a soft-iron core. Radial field means the plane of the coil is always parallel to B, so torque NIAB doesn't depend on deflection. A spring provides a restoring torque kφ. At equilibrium:

NIAB = kφ  ⇒  φ = (NAB/k) I

Deflection is proportional to current — a linear scale.

- **Current sensitivity** = φ/I = NAB/k.
- **Voltage sensitivity** = φ/V = NAB/(kR_G).
Doubling N doubles current sensitivity but also doubles R_G, so voltage sensitivity is unchanged.

**Converting to an ammeter:** put a small **shunt** S in parallel. If the galvanometer's full-scale current is I_g and you want range I: S = I_g G/(I − I_g). The ammeter has very low resistance and goes in series.

**Converting to a voltmeter:** put a large resistance R in series: R = V/I_g − G. The voltmeter has very high resistance and goes in parallel, so it barely disturbs the circuit.

check.q: A galvanometer (G = 50 Ω, full scale 5 mA) is to read 0–5 A. The shunt needed is about:

parts.md: At a scrap yard on the outskirts of Ludhiana, Arjun watched a crane lower a giant disc onto a heap of old bicycle frames. A hum, and the frames leapt up and clung. The operator swung the arm over a truck, and with a click the frames clattered down. 'No hook, no rope?' Arjun asked. The operator tapped the cable: 'Only current, beta.' The disc was a huge coil wrapped around an iron core — a solenoid's cousin. Turn on hundreds of amperes, and B = μ₀nI inside, multiplied many times by the iron, magnetises the steel scrap so it is pulled toward the pole.

Arjun asked why it didn't hold on after switch-off. 'Soft iron,' said the operator. Arjun later found out in Chapter 5 that soft iron has low retentivity — it loses magnetisation easily — which is exactly what a crane needs. He also realised the scrap still felt only a force on its magnetisation, while the moving electrons in the coil felt the Lorentz force that made the coil itself strain against its mount. 'Moving charges make magnetism' had stopped being a sentence in a book; it was lifting a tonne of steel.

sections.h: The direction rules, once and for all
sections.md:
Part 1 covered the full chapter: Oersted's discovery, the Lorentz force, circular and helical motion and the velocity selector, the Biot–Savart law and a loop's field, Ampere's law with solenoids and toroids, the force between parallel currents, torque on a loop and the moving-coil galvanometer.

Most lost marks in this chapter are **direction** errors, so begin there.

- **Force on a moving charge:** F = q(v × B). Point the fingers of the right hand along v, curl them towards B; the thumb gives F for a **positive** charge. Reverse it for an electron.
- **Field of a straight wire:** grip the wire with the right thumb along the current; the fingers curl in the direction of B (concentric circles).
- **Field of a loop:** curl the fingers along the current; the thumb points along B at the centre (the loop's north face).
- **Force on a wire:** F = I(l × B), same rule as a positive charge moving along I.

**Symbols:** ⊙ = out of the page (arrow tip), ⊗ = into the page (arrow tail).

*Quick test.* A proton moves east in a field pointing vertically up. v × B: east × up = north... check: with x = east, y = north, z = up, x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ, so the force is towards the **south**. An electron moving east would be pushed north.

> **Did you know?** The aurora over the Arctic is charged particles from the Sun spiralling along Earth's magnetic field lines into the upper atmosphere near the poles — helical motion on a planetary scale.

**Circular orbit (v ⟂ B):** qvB = mv²/r ⇒ **r = mv/(qB)**, period T = 2πm/(qB), frequency ν = qB/(2πm) — independent of speed. This speed-independence is what makes the cyclotron work.

*Problem.* An electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moves at 3.0 × 10⁷ m/s perpendicular to B = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ T. r = (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 3.0 × 10⁷)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.73 × 10⁻²³/9.6 × 10⁻²³ ≈ **0.28 m** = 28 cm. ν = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6.0 × 10⁻⁴)/(2π × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹) ≈ **1.7 × 10⁷ Hz**.

*Problem (energy given).* An electron accelerated through 2.0 kV enters a 0.15 T field at right angles. Speed: ½mv² = eV ⇒ v = √(2eV/m) = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2000/9.1 × 10⁻³¹) ≈ 2.65 × 10⁷ m/s. r = mv/(eB) ≈ (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.65 × 10⁷)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.15) ≈ **1.0 × 10⁻³ m**.

**Helix (v at angle θ to B):** v∥ = v cos θ is untouched, v⟂ = v sin θ makes circles. Radius r = mv sin θ/(qB); **pitch** p = v cos θ · T = 2πmv cos θ/(qB).

**Velocity selector:** crossed E and B pass only particles with **v = E/B** undeflected, whatever their charge or mass.

**Does the magnetic force do work?** No. F ⟂ v always, so the speed and kinetic energy never change; only the direction does.

sections.h: Fields of wires, loops, solenoids and toroids
sections.md:
| Source | Field |
|---|---|
| Long straight wire, distance r | B = μ₀I/(2πr) |
| Centre of circular loop, radius R, N turns | B = μ₀NI/(2R) |
| On axis of loop, distance x | B = μ₀NIR²/(2(x² + R²)^(3/2)) |
| Long solenoid, n turns per metre | B = μ₀nI (inside), ≈ 0 outside |
| Toroid, N turns, mean radius r | B = μ₀NI/(2πr) inside the core, 0 outside |

μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.

*Wire.* 35 A in a long straight wire: at 20 cm, B = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 35)/(2π × 0.20) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 35/0.20 = **3.5 × 10⁻⁵ T**.

*Coil.* 100 turns, radius 8.0 cm, 0.40 A: B = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 100 × 0.40)/(2 × 0.08) = (5.03 × 10⁻⁵)/0.16 ≈ **3.1 × 10⁻⁴ T**.

*Solenoid.* 80 cm long, 5 layers of 400 turns (N = 2000), 8.0 A: n = 2000/0.8 = 2500 m⁻¹. B = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2500 × 8 ≈ **2.5 × 10⁻² T**.

*Toroid.* Mean radius 25 cm, 3500 turns, 11 A: B = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 3500 × 11)/(2π × 0.25) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 38 500/0.25 ≈ **3.1 × 10⁻² T**.

**Ampere's law** ∮B · dl = μ₀I_enclosed works best when symmetry lets B be constant along a chosen loop — a circle round a wire, a rectangle half inside a solenoid, a circle inside a toroid.

check.q: Doubling both the current and the distance from a long straight wire changes B by a factor of:
check.why: B = μ₀I/(2πr): doubling I doubles B, doubling r halves it, so the field is unchanged.

sections.md:
**Wire in a field:** F = BIl sin θ.
*Problem.* A 3.0 cm wire carrying 10 A is placed inside a solenoid (B = 0.27 T) perpendicular to its axis: F = 0.27 × 10 × 0.03 = **8.1 × 10⁻² N**.

**Parallel wires:** force per unit length f = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd); **like currents attract, unlike repel**.
*Problem.* Two wires 4.0 cm apart carry 8.0 A and 5.0 A in the same direction: f = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 40/0.04 = 2 × 10⁻⁴ N/m, attractive. On a 10 cm section: **2 × 10⁻⁵ N**.
This force once defined the ampere: 1 A in each of two wires 1 m apart gives 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre. (Since 2019 the ampere is defined by fixing the electron's charge, but the force relation still holds.)

**Torque on a loop:** τ = NIAB sin θ = m × B, where **m = NIA** is the magnetic moment and θ is the angle between the loop's normal and B. Maximum when the plane of the loop is parallel to B.
*Problem.* A 100-turn, 10 cm × 5 cm (A = 5 × 10⁻³ m²) coil carries 2 A in 0.5 T, plane parallel to B: τ = 100 × 2 × 5 × 10⁻³ × 0.5 = **0.5 N m**.

**Orbiting electron as a dipole:** an electron circling a nucleus is a tiny current loop. Its magnetic moment μ_l = (e/2m_e)L; for the lowest Bohr orbit this is the **Bohr magneton**, about 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ A m².

check.why: Each wire's field at the other produces a force directed away when the currents are antiparallel.

sections.md:
In a moving-coil galvanometer the deflecting torque NIAB is balanced by the spring's restoring torque kφ, so **I = (k/NAB)φ** — the scale is linear because a radial field from curved pole pieces and a soft-iron core keeps the plane of the coil parallel to B.

**Current sensitivity** φ/I = NAB/k; **voltage sensitivity** φ/V = NAB/(kR_G). Doubling N doubles current sensitivity but, since the coil's resistance also roughly doubles, voltage sensitivity may not change.

**To an ammeter:** put a small **shunt** S in parallel: S = I_g G/(I − I_g).
*Problem.* G = 12 Ω, full scale at 3 mA, convert to 0–6 A: S = (3 × 10⁻³ × 12)/(6 − 0.003) ≈ **6 × 10⁻³ Ω** (6 mΩ) in parallel.

**To a voltmeter:** add a large resistance R in **series**: R = V/I_g − G.
*Problem.* Same galvanometer to 0–18 V: R = 18/(3 × 10⁻³) − 12 = 6000 − 12 = **5988 Ω** in series.

An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance, so that inserting them disturbs the circuit as little as possible.

check.q: To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter you connect:
check.why: A large series resistance limits the current to I_g at the full-scale voltage and keeps the meter from loading the circuit.

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch05-magnetism-m.title: Magnetism and Matter
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch05-magnetism-m.subtitle: Why a frog can levitate, iron sticks, and copper politely refuses

sections.h: 1. A magnet you can't cut in half
sections.md:
Take a bar magnet and break it in the middle. You don't get a separate north pole and south pole — you get two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S. Break again and again, right down to single atoms, and still every piece is a complete magnet. No one has ever found an isolated magnetic pole (a **monopole**).

That single fact is the heart of this chapter. In Chapter 4 we learnt that current loops behave like magnets. Here we turn it around: magnets — and magnetic materials — behave as they do because of countless tiny current loops (electron orbits and spins) inside atoms.

Basic properties you met in earlier classes still hold:
- A freely suspended magnet points roughly north–south.
- Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
- Field lines emerge from the N pole outside the magnet and enter at S, but **continue inside** from S to N, forming closed loops.
- Field lines never cross, and their density shows field strength.

check.q: Magnetic field lines of a bar magnet:
options: start at N and end at S
cross each other near the poles
check.why: Since there are no monopoles, field lines have no beginning or end; they close through the magnet from S to N.

sections.h: 2. The bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
sections.md:
Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet and around a current-carrying solenoid make almost identical patterns. Far away, the field of both is that of a **magnetic dipole** with moment **m** (pointing from S to N).

For a dipole, at distance r large compared with its size:
- **Axial point (end-on):** B = (μ₀/4π) · 2m / r³
- **Equatorial point (broadside-on):** B = −(μ₀/4π) · m / r³ (opposite to m)

Compare with the electric dipole: the forms are identical with p → m and 1/ε₀ → μ₀. The axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance.

**Dipole in a uniform field.** A magnet with moment m in field B feels torque **τ = m × B** (magnitude mB sin θ) and has potential energy **U = −m · B = −mB cos θ**. Energy is minimum (stable equilibrium) at θ = 0 and maximum (unstable) at θ = 180°.

If you displace a compass needle slightly and let go, it oscillates. For small angles the motion is simple harmonic with period

T = 2π √(I / mB)

where I is the moment of inertia. Timing the oscillations lets you measure mB — a classic experiment.

check.q: The ratio of the magnetic field at an axial point to that at an equatorial point at the same large distance from a short magnet is:
check.why: Axial B = (μ₀/4π)2m/r³ and equatorial B = (μ₀/4π)m/r³, so the ratio is 2:1.

sections.md:
In electrostatics, the flux of E through a closed surface equals q_enclosed/ε₀. For magnetism the corresponding statement is beautifully simple:

**∮ B · dS = 0**

The net magnetic flux through *any* closed surface is zero. Every field line that enters a closed surface also leaves it. This is the mathematical way of saying *there are no magnetic monopoles*.

If you draw a surface around just the N end of a bar magnet, the lines leaving outward are exactly balanced by the lines entering from inside the magnet. Physicists have searched for monopoles in cosmic rays and accelerators; none has been confirmed.

check.q: Gauss's law for magnetism implies:
options: isolated magnetic poles do not exist
B is zero inside a magnet
check.why: Zero net flux through every closed surface means no surface can enclose a net 'magnetic charge', so monopoles don't exist.

sections.md:
Place a material inside a solenoid with field B₀ = μ₀nI. The atoms' tiny dipoles respond, and the field inside changes. To describe this we define:

- **Magnetisation M**: net magnetic moment per unit volume, M = m_net / V (unit A/m).
- **Magnetic intensity H**: the part of the field due to free currents, H = B/μ₀ − M. For a solenoid, H = nI (unit A/m).

So the total field is

**B = μ₀ (H + M)**

For most materials M is proportional to H: **M = χ H**, where χ (chi) is the dimensionless **magnetic susceptibility**. Then

B = μ₀(1 + χ)H = μ₀ μ_r H = μ H

with **relative permeability μ_r = 1 + χ** and permeability μ = μ₀μ_r.

The sign and size of χ classify materials:

| Class | χ | μ_r | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Diamagnetic | small, negative (~−10⁻⁵) | slightly < 1 | bismuth, copper, water, gold |
| Paramagnetic | small, positive (~10⁻⁵–10⁻³) | slightly > 1 | aluminium, sodium, oxygen |
| Ferromagnetic | large, positive (10²–10⁵) | ≫ 1 | iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium |
keyTerms: Magnetisation M — dipole moment per unit volume
Magnetic intensity H — field from free currents, H = nI in a solenoid
Susceptibility χ — M/H
Relative permeability μ_r — 1 + χ

check.q: A material has susceptibility χ = −2 × 10⁻⁵. It is:
check.why: A small negative susceptibility is the signature of diamagnetism.

sections.md:
In diamagnetic atoms, electron moments cancel in pairs; the atom has no permanent dipole. When an external field is applied, electron orbits adjust (a consequence of induction, Chapter 6) to produce a small moment **opposite** to the field. Result:
- Weakly repelled by a magnet; moves from strong to weak field regions.
- Field lines are slightly pushed out of the material.
- A diamagnetic liquid in a U-tube between magnet poles goes *down* on the pole side.
- Susceptibility nearly independent of temperature.

Diamagnetism is present in **all** materials, but usually masked by stronger effects. In a very strong magnet (about 16 T), even water's weak diamagnetism can levitate a live frog — a famous Ig Nobel experiment from 1997.

**Superconductors** are perfect diamagnets: χ = −1, μ_r = 0. They expel the field completely (the **Meissner effect**), which lets maglev trains float.

check.q: A superconductor in its superconducting state has relative permeability:
check.why: It is a perfect diamagnet with χ = −1, so μ_r = 1 + χ = 0.

sections.md:
Paramagnetic atoms *do* have permanent dipoles (unpaired electrons), but thermal motion scatters their directions randomly. An external field partly aligns them, giving a small magnetisation **along** the field.
- Weakly attracted; moves from weak to strong field regions.
- Field lines slightly concentrated inside.
- Liquid in a U-tube rises on the pole side. (Liquid oxygen clings between magnet poles!)

Heat fights alignment, so susceptibility falls with temperature. **Curie's law**:

M = C (B₀ / T),  or χ = C μ₀ / T

where C is the Curie constant and T the absolute temperature. At very low temperature and strong field, magnetisation saturates when all dipoles are aligned.

check.q: By Curie's law, if the absolute temperature of a paramagnetic sample doubles, its susceptibility:
check.why: χ ∝ 1/T, so doubling T halves χ.

sections.md:
In iron, cobalt and nickel, neighbouring atomic dipoles interact strongly (a quantum effect) and line up spontaneously within regions called **domains**, each about 1 mm or smaller, containing ~10¹⁷–10¹⁸ atoms. In an unmagnetised piece, domains point in random directions. An external field makes favourably aligned domains grow (domain walls move) and others rotate. The result is a huge magnetisation.

Above the **Curie temperature T_c**, thermal agitation destroys the alignment and the material becomes paramagnetic, with χ = C/(T − T_c). For iron, T_c ≈ 1043 K (770 °C); for nickel about 631 K.

**Hysteresis.** Magnetise iron by raising H: B rises along a curve and saturates. Reduce H to zero: B doesn't return to zero — a **retentivity (remanence)** remains. You must apply reverse H, the **coercivity**, to bring B to zero. Cycling gives a loop; its area is the energy lost as heat per cycle per unit volume.

- **Hard ferromagnets** (alnico, neodymium magnets): high retentivity, high coercivity — **permanent magnets** for speakers, motors, fridge doors.
- **Soft ferromagnets** (soft iron): low coercivity, narrow loop — for **electromagnets and transformer cores**, which are magnetised and demagnetised 50 times every second on India's 50 Hz grid.

*(Earth's magnetism — declination, dip and the geomagnetic field — appeared in older editions of this chapter; it is no longer in the rationalised NCERT syllabus, but it's a lovely topic: Earth's field is about 3–5 × 10⁻⁵ T and is generated by currents in the molten outer core.)*

check.q: Transformer cores are made of soft iron mainly because it has:
options: low coercivity and small hysteresis loss
check.why: A narrow hysteresis loop means little energy lost as heat each cycle when the core is repeatedly magnetised.

workedExamples.q: A short bar magnet of moment 0.40 A·m² is placed in a uniform field of 0.16 T. Find the torque at 30° and the work to turn it from 0° to 180°.
Find B at 10 cm on the axis of a short magnet of moment 0.5 A·m².

summary: Magnetic poles always come in pairs; field lines form closed loops.
A bar magnet is equivalent to a solenoid; both are magnetic dipoles with moment m (S→N).
Axial B = (μ₀/4π)2m/r³; equatorial B = (μ₀/4π)m/r³.
Torque τ = m×B; potential energy U = −m·B; oscillation T = 2π√(I/mB).
Gauss's law for magnetism: ∮B·dS = 0 — no monopoles.
B = μ₀(H + M); M = χH; μ_r = 1 + χ.
Diamagnets: χ small negative, repelled, T-independent; superconductors are perfect diamagnets.
Paramagnets: χ small positive, Curie's law χ ∝ 1/T.
Ferromagnets: domains, huge χ, become paramagnetic above the Curie temperature.
Hysteresis: retentivity and coercivity; hard magnets for permanent magnets, soft iron for cores.

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch05-magnetism-m.title: Magnetism and Matter — Part 2: Dipoles at Work, Materials in Numbers
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch05-magnetism-m.subtitle: Field lines, dipole fields, torque and oscillation, the electrostatics analogy, Curie's law and choosing magnet materials

sections.md:
Part 1 told the chapter's story: you cannot isolate a magnetic pole; a bar magnet behaves like a solenoid; Gauss's law for magnetism says the net flux through any closed surface is zero; and materials respond to fields as diamagnets, paramagnets or ferromagnets, described by magnetisation M, intensity H and susceptibility χ, with domains and hysteresis.

Part 2 adds the remaining pieces of the chapter, with numbers:

1. Properties of **magnetic field lines**.
2. The **dipole field** on the axis and the equator, and the **electrostatic analogy**.
3. A **dipole in a uniform field** — torque, potential energy and small oscillations.
4. **Relations between B, H and M** with numerical examples.
5. **Curie's law** and temperature effects.
6. **Permanent magnets and electromagnets** — how hysteresis decides the material.

> **Did you know?** Earth itself is a giant magnet whose 'north magnetic pole' (near northern Canada) is actually a *south* pole of the Earth's magnet — that is why a compass's north-seeking end points there. The field is thought to come from currents in the molten outer core.

Field lines are a picture, not physical strings, but they obey strict rules:

1. They form **continuous closed loops** — out of the north pole outside the magnet, back from south to north inside. (Electric field lines, in contrast, begin and end on charges.)
2. The **tangent** at any point gives the direction of B there.
3. The **density** of lines (number crossing unit area at right angles) shows the field's strength — crowded near the poles, sparse far away.
4. Lines **never intersect**: if they did, B would have two directions at one point.

These rules let you check diagrams quickly. A drawing with lines starting from nowhere, crossing, or not closing is wrong. In the chapter's exercises you are often shown sketches and asked which are impossible — apply these four rules.

**Iron filings and compasses.** Sprinkle filings on a card over a bar magnet: they line up along the field, revealing loops. A small compass placed anywhere aligns its axis along the tangent.

**Neutral points.** Where the magnet's field exactly cancels another field (such as the Earth's horizontal field), the net field is zero, and a compass there shows no preferred direction.

check.q: Which statement about magnetic field lines is FALSE?
options: They can intersect at the poles
check.why: Two lines crossing would mean two directions of B at one point, which is impossible anywhere, including near poles.

sections.h: The dipole field and the electric analogy
sections.md:
For a short bar magnet (or any current loop) of magnetic moment m, at distance r much larger than its size:

- **Axial point:** B_A = (μ₀/4π)(2m/r³), along m.
- **Equatorial point:** B_E = (μ₀/4π)(m/r³), opposite to m.

The axial field is **twice** the equatorial field at the same distance, and both fall as 1/r³.

**The analogy.** Every result for an electric dipole p in Chapter 1 becomes a magnetic result with the swaps:

| Electrostatics | Magnetism |
|---|---|
| 1/ε₀ | μ₀ |
| dipole moment p | magnetic moment m |
| E (axial) = 2p/(4πε₀r³) | B (axial) = μ₀2m/(4πr³) |
| torque p × E | torque m × B |
| energy −p · E | energy −m · B |

*Problem.* A short bar magnet of moment 0.48 J/T. Field at 10 cm on its axis: B = 10⁻⁷ × 2 × 0.48/(0.1)³ = 10⁻⁷ × 0.96/10⁻³ = **9.6 × 10⁻⁵ T**, along the S → N direction. On the equator at 10 cm: **4.8 × 10⁻⁵ T**, opposite.

*Solenoid as magnet.* A solenoid of 800 turns, cross-section 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m², current 3.0 A: m = NIA = 800 × 3 × 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = **0.60 A m²** (J/T) — it behaves exactly like a bar magnet of that moment.

check.q: At equal distance, the axial field of a short magnet compared with its equatorial field is:
check.why: B_axial = (μ₀/4π)(2m/r³) while B_equatorial = (μ₀/4π)(m/r³).

sections.h: A dipole in a uniform field: torque, energy and oscillation
sections.md:
**Torque** τ = m × B, magnitude **mB sin θ**, tends to align m with B.

**Potential energy** U = −m · B = −mB cos θ.
- θ = 0°: U = −mB, **stable** equilibrium (minimum energy).
- θ = 180°: U = +mB, **unstable** equilibrium.
- Work to turn from θ₁ to θ₂: W = mB(cos θ₁ − cos θ₂). From 0° to 180°: W = 2mB.

*Problem.* A magnet of moment 0.32 J/T in 0.15 T. Stable orientation energy = −0.048 J; unstable = +0.048 J. Torque when at 30°: 0.32 × 0.15 × 0.5 = **0.024 N m**.

**Oscillations.** Displace a freely suspended magnet slightly; the restoring torque −mBθ gives simple harmonic motion with

**T = 2π√(I/(mB))**,

where I is its moment of inertia. Measure T and you can find m or B. This is how the horizontal component of the Earth's field has historically been measured with a vibration magnetometer.

*Problem.* A compass needle with I = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ kg m² oscillates in a field of 0.01 T... suppose its period is 0.665 s. Then mB = 4π²I/T² ⇒ m = 4π² × 6.0 × 10⁻⁷/(0.665² × 0.01) ≈ 2.37 × 10⁻⁵/4.42 × 10⁻³ ≈ **5.4 × 10⁻³ J/T**.

*Why a magnet in a non-uniform field also feels a net force:* the two 'poles' feel different strengths, so besides torque there is a pull towards stronger field — this is why iron nails jump towards a magnet.

check.q: The work done to rotate a dipole from θ = 0° to 180° in field B is:
check.why: W = mB(cos 0° − cos 180°) = mB(1 + 1) = 2mB.

sections.h: B, H and M with numbers
sections.md:
Inside a material, **B = μ₀(H + M)**, where H is the field due to free currents (for a solenoid H = nI) and M is the magnetisation (magnetic moment per unit volume).

For linear materials **M = χH**, so **B = μ₀(1 + χ)H = μ₀μ_rH = μH**, with relative permeability μ_r = 1 + χ.

| Class | χ | μ_r | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Diamagnetic | small, negative (~ −10⁻⁵) | slightly < 1 | bismuth, copper, water, superconductors (χ = −1) |
| Paramagnetic | small, positive (~10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³) | slightly > 1 | aluminium, sodium, oxygen |
| Ferromagnetic | large, positive (10³ or more) | ≫ 1 | iron, cobalt, nickel, alnico |

*Problem.* A solenoid has a core of relative permeability 400; n = 1000 turns/m, I = 2 A.
H = nI = **2000 A/m**. B = μ_rμ₀H = 400 × 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 ≈ **1.0 T**. χ = μ_r − 1 = 399, M = χH ≈ **8.0 × 10⁵ A/m**. Notice that almost all of B comes from the magnetised core, not the current.

**Superconductors** expel magnetic fields completely (the Meissner effect): perfect diamagnets. This is what lets a magnet float above a cold superconductor and powers maglev demonstrations.

check.q: For a material with μ_r = 400, the susceptibility χ is:

sections.h: Curie's law and the effect of temperature
sections.md:
In a **paramagnet**, atomic dipoles want to align with the field, but thermal jiggling scrambles them. The hotter it is, the weaker the alignment:

**χ = C μ₀/T** (Curie's law), where C is the Curie constant and T the absolute temperature.

*Problem.* A paramagnetic salt has 8% of its maximum (saturation) magnetisation at 0.84 T and 4.2 K. What would it be at 0.98 T and 2.8 K? For weak alignment M ∝ B/T: M₂/M₁ = (B₂/B₁)(T₁/T₂) = (0.98/0.84)(4.2/2.8) = 1.167 × 1.5 = 1.75. So M₂ ≈ 1.75 × 8% = **14%** of saturation.

**Ferromagnets and the Curie temperature.** Above a critical temperature T_c, thermal motion breaks up the domains and a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic. Above T_c, χ = C/(T − T_c). Iron's Curie temperature is about 1043 K (770 °C); nickel's about 631 K; cobalt's about 1394 K. A heated iron nail falls off a magnet when it gets hot enough — a classroom demonstration of T_c.

**Diamagnetism** is almost independent of temperature, because it comes from induced orbital currents, not from aligning existing dipoles.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fff9f2'/><line x1='60' y1='220' x2='560' y2='220' stroke='#555'/><line x1='60' y1='20' x2='60' y2='220' stroke='#555'/><path d='M80,30 C120,150 220,190 540,210' fill='none' stroke='#d84315' stroke-width='4' stroke-dasharray='600' stroke-dashoffset='600'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='600;0' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' fill='#222'><text x='300' y='245'>temperature T →</text><text x='70' y='15'>χ</text><text x='250' y='120'>χ ∝ 1/T (Curie's law)</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: A paramagnet's susceptibility falls as temperature rises — the curve draws itself as heat scrambles the dipoles.
fig.alt: Falling curve of susceptibility versus temperature drawing itself.

check.q: If the absolute temperature of a paramagnet doubles (same field), its magnetisation:
check.why: Curie's law gives χ ∝ 1/T, so M = χH falls to half.

sections.md:
The **hysteresis loop** (B against H as H is cycled) tells you what a ferromagnet is good for. Two numbers matter: **retentivity** (B left when H returns to zero) and **coercivity** (reverse H needed to bring B to zero). The **area** of the loop is the energy lost as heat per cycle per unit volume.

| Use | Needs | Material |
|---|---|---|
| Permanent magnet (speakers, motors, fridge seals) | high retentivity, **high coercivity** | steel, alnico, cobalt steel, ticonal; modern NdFeB |
| Electromagnet (cranes, relays, MRI iron) | high permeability, **low coercivity**, low retentivity | soft iron |
| Transformer and motor cores | **thin loop** (low hysteresis loss), high resistivity | soft iron, silicon steel, ferrites |

**Why soft iron, not steel, for an electromagnet?** It magnetises strongly when current flows and loses most of its magnetism when the current stops — exactly what a scrap-yard crane needs to drop its load.

**Making a permanent magnet.** Place a steel rod inside a solenoid and pass a strong current; the domains align and stay aligned. Or stroke it repeatedly with one pole of another magnet (the old method).

> **Did you know?** The world's strongest commercial permanent magnets, neodymium–iron–boron, are in phone speakers, earbuds and the motors of electric scooters made in India.

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch06-electromagn.title: Electromagnetic Induction
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch06-electromagn.subtitle: Move a magnet, get a current — the trick that powers every city on Earth

sections.h: 1. If current makes magnetism, can magnetism make current?
sections.md:
After Ørsted showed that currents produce magnetic fields, scientists naturally asked the reverse question. Placing a magnet next to a wire did nothing. The breakthrough came in 1831 when **Michael Faraday** in England (and independently **Joseph Henry** in the USA) discovered the secret: it is not the field but the **change** in field that produces current.

Every thermal, hydro and nuclear power station — from Tehri dam to Kudankulam — works on this principle. A turbine spins a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet near coils), and the changing magnetic flux drives current into the grid. Induction cooktops, wireless phone chargers, metal detectors at airports and the pickups in an electric guitar all use it too.

check.q: Electromagnetic induction was discovered independently by:
check.why: Faraday and Henry independently discovered in the early 1830s that changing magnetic fields induce currents.

sections.h: 2. The experiments of Faraday and Henry
sections.md:
Three classic experiments sum up the discovery:

1. **Magnet and coil.** Connect a coil to a galvanometer. Push a bar magnet's N pole toward the coil: the needle deflects. Hold it still: no deflection. Pull it away: deflection the other way. Push faster: bigger deflection. Moving the coil instead of the magnet gives the same result — only *relative motion* matters.
2. **Two coils.** Replace the magnet with a second coil carrying a steady current. Moving either coil induces current in the other.
3. **Switching.** Keep both coils still. At the instant you close the key in the primary, the galvanometer in the secondary kicks; while the current stays steady, nothing; when you open the key, it kicks the other way. An iron rod through both coils makes the kick much larger.

The common factor in all three: the **magnetic flux** through the coil is changing.

check.q: In Faraday's two-coil experiment, the galvanometer in the secondary deflects:
options: only while the primary current is steady
only when the primary current is switched on or off
check.why: Induced emf requires changing flux, which occurs only as the primary current rises or falls.

sections.md:
**Magnetic flux** through a plane area A in uniform field B is

Φ_B = B · A = B A cos θ

where θ is the angle between B and the area's normal. Unit: **weber (Wb)** = T·m². For non-uniform fields we sum: Φ_B = Σ B·dA.

**Faraday's law of induction:** the magnitude of the induced emf equals the rate of change of magnetic flux. For a coil of N turns:

**ε = −N dΦ_B / dt**

The flux can change in three ways: change B, change A, or change θ (rotate the coil). The minus sign is Lenz's law, coming next.

If the coil's circuit has resistance R, induced current I = ε/R, and the total charge that flows is Q = NΔΦ/R — independent of how fast the change happened.
keyTerms: Magnetic flux Φ = BA cos θ, unit weber
Faraday's law — ε = −N dΦ/dt

check.q: A 100-turn coil's flux changes from 0.05 Wb to 0.01 Wb in 0.2 s. The magnitude of induced emf is:

sections.h: 4. Lenz's law and conservation of energy
sections.md:
**Lenz's law (1834):** the induced current flows in a direction that *opposes the change* in flux that produced it.

Push a magnet's N pole toward a coil: the coil's near face becomes an N pole to repel it (current anticlockwise as seen from the magnet). Pull the N pole away: the near face becomes S, attracting it back. Either way, you must do work against the induced effect.

This isn't an extra rule bolted on — it's **energy conservation**. If the induced current *helped* the change, the magnet would accelerate by itself, the current would grow, and you'd get unlimited energy from nothing. The work you do pushing the magnet against the opposition is exactly what appears as electrical energy (and then heat) in the coil.

A striking demonstration: drop a strong neodymium magnet down a copper pipe. It drifts down slowly, as if through honey, because the currents induced in the pipe oppose its motion.

check.why: If induced currents aided the change, energy would be created from nothing; opposition ensures the work done becomes electrical energy.

sections.md:
Slide a conducting rod of length l with speed v on two rails, perpendicular to a uniform field B. The area of the circuit grows at rate lv, so dΦ/dt = Blv and

**ε = B l v**

We can also see this from the Lorentz force. Each free charge in the moving rod feels a force qvB along the rod, pushing charges to one end. The work per unit charge over length l is vBl — the same emf.

With a resistor R completing the circuit, current I = Blv/R flows. The rod then feels a magnetic force F = IlB = B²l²v/R *opposing* the motion (Lenz again). To keep v constant you must push with this force, delivering power P = Fv = B²l²v²/R — exactly equal to the Joule heat I²R. Energy is conserved perfectly.

**Rotating rod:** a rod of length l spinning with angular velocity ω about one end perpendicular to B develops ε = ½ B ω l².

check.q: A 0.5 m rod moves at 4 m/s perpendicular to a 0.2 T field. The emf is:

sections.md:
*(Eddy currents were removed from the rationalised NCERT chapter, but you'll meet them in any real machine: they are the swirling currents induced in bulk metal, used in induction cooktops and electromagnetic brakes in trains, and minimised by laminating transformer cores.)*

**Mutual inductance.** A current I₁ in coil 1 creates flux through coil 2: N₂Φ₂ = M I₁. When I₁ changes, coil 2 gets an emf

ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt

M (unit **henry**, H) depends on geometry, turns and core. For two long coaxial solenoids (inner radius r₁, length l, turns per length n₁ and n₂):

M = μ₀ n₁ n₂ π r₁² l

It's symmetric: M₁₂ = M₂₁. A soft-iron core multiplies M by μ_r.

**Self-inductance.** A coil's own changing current changes its own flux: NΦ = LI, so

ε = −L dI/dt

This **back emf** opposes changes in current — inductance is electrical inertia. For a long solenoid of n turns per length, area A, length l:

L = μ₀ n² A l  (times μ_r with a core)

**Energy stored in an inductor:** building current I against the back emf takes work

U = ½ L I²

— the twin of ½mv² for a moving mass and ½CV² for a capacitor. This energy lives in the magnetic field, with energy density u = B²/(2μ₀). That's why switching off a big motor can make a spark at the switch: the stored energy has to go somewhere.
keyTerms: Mutual inductance M — flux linkage in one coil per unit current in another
Self-inductance L — flux linkage per unit own current
Henry — 1 V·s/A

check.q: The energy stored in a 0.2 H inductor carrying 3 A is:

sections.md:
A coil of N turns and area A rotates with angular speed ω in a uniform field B. The angle between B and the normal is θ = ωt, so

Φ = NBA cos ωt  ⇒  ε = NBAω sin ωt = ε₀ sin ωt

with peak emf **ε₀ = NBAω**. The emf is sinusoidal: zero when the coil plane is perpendicular to B (flux maximum), maximum when the plane is parallel to B (flux zero but changing fastest).

Slip rings and brushes carry the current out without tangling the wires. In India the grid frequency is **50 Hz**, so ω = 2π × 50 ≈ 314 rad/s. Large generators keep the coils fixed (stator) and rotate an electromagnet (rotor) instead — the physics is identical. A hydro turbine at Bhakra, a steam turbine at a thermal plant or a wind turbine in Tamil Nadu just provides the mechanical turning.

parts.md: In Kanpur in the 1990s, Riya's father had a black bicycle with a little bottle-shaped dynamo pressed against the rear tyre. When he pedalled slowly the front lamp glowed a dull orange; on the downhill slope near the railway crossing it blazed white. And whenever the lamp was on, pedalling felt a little heavier. Years later, studying this chapter, Riya finally understood all three facts.

Inside the dynamo, a small magnet spun inside a coil. Faster pedalling meant larger ω and so larger ε₀ = NBAω — a brighter lamp. And the extra effort? Lenz's law. The current in the coil made its own field that opposed the magnet's rotation; her father's legs supplied the energy that the lamp turned into light and heat. 'So Papa was the power station,' she laughed, 'and the coil was charging him for every watt.'

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch06-electromagn.title: Electromagnetic Induction — Part 2: Flux, Lenz and Inductance in Practice
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch06-electromagn.subtitle: Every exercise type — changing flux, Lenz directions, moving rods, eddy currents, inductors and generators — worked in full

sections.h: The one idea behind the whole chapter
sections.md:
Part 1 followed the chapter: Faraday's and Henry's experiments, magnetic flux and Faraday's law, Lenz's law and energy, motional emf, self- and mutual inductance and the AC generator.

Everything rests on one sentence: **an emf is induced whenever the magnetic flux through a circuit changes**, and ε = −dΦ/dt (or −N dΦ/dt for N turns). Flux Φ = BA cos θ can change in three ways:

1. **B changes** — a magnet moves, or a nearby current is switched.
2. **A changes** — a rod slides on rails, a loop is stretched or pulled out of a field.
3. **θ changes** — a coil rotates (the generator).

Part 2 practises each, then adds **eddy currents** (a section of the chapter not yet covered in depth), **energy stored in an inductor**, and mixed numericals.

> **Did you know?** Michael Faraday announced his discovery of induction in 1831; Joseph Henry in the USA had observed it independently at about the same time. The unit of capacitance (farad) and of inductance (henry) honour them.

*B changing.* A square loop of side 10 cm, resistance 0.5 Ω, sits with its plane perpendicular to a field that falls uniformly from 0.1 T to 0 in 0.70 s. Φᵢ = 0.1 × 0.01 = 10⁻³ Wb. |ε| = 10⁻³/0.70 ≈ **1.43 × 10⁻³ V**; I = 2.86 mA.

*Current switched off in a coil.* A long solenoid (n = 15 turns/cm = 1500 m⁻¹) carries 2.0 A; a small 100-turn loop of area 2.0 cm² sits inside, coaxial. The current falls to zero in 0.1 s. B = μ₀nI = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1500 × 2 ≈ 3.77 × 10⁻³ T. Φ per turn = 3.77 × 10⁻³ × 2 × 10⁻⁴ = 7.54 × 10⁻⁷ Wb. ε = 100 × 7.54 × 10⁻⁷/0.1 ≈ **7.5 × 10⁻⁴ V**.

*Flux as a function of time.* If Φ = 6t² − 5t + 1 (weber, t in s), then |ε| = 12t − 5; at t = 0.25 s, |ε| = 2 V.

*Charge through the circuit.* Integrating I = ε/R gives **Q = ΔΦ/R** (times N) — independent of how fast the change happens. Pull a coil out of a field slowly or quickly: the same charge flows, though the current differs.

*Problem.* A 50-turn coil of area 0.02 m² and resistance 5 Ω is flipped (θ 0° → 180°) in a 0.1 T field. ΔΦ per turn = 2BA = 4 × 10⁻³ Wb. Q = 50 × 4 × 10⁻³/5 = **0.04 C**.

check.q: The charge that flows when the flux through a coil changes depends on:
