check.why: Q = NΔΦ/R: speed affects the current but not the total charge.

sections.md:
**Lenz's law:** the induced current flows so as to **oppose the change** that produces it.

Recipe: (1) Which way is the flux through the loop? (2) Is it increasing or decreasing? (3) The induced current makes its own field **opposite** to the original if increasing, **along** it if decreasing. (4) Use the right-hand loop rule to turn that field into a current direction.

*Magnet approaching.* North pole pushed towards a coil: flux towards the coil increases, so the near face of the coil becomes a **north** pole to repel — current anticlockwise as seen from the magnet. Pull it away: the near face becomes a **south** pole to attract it back — clockwise.

*Loop leaving a field.* A rectangular loop is pulled out of a field pointing into the page. Inward flux decreases, so the induced current tries to keep it: it produces an **inward** field inside, i.e. **clockwise** current.

*Two coils.* Closing a switch in coil P (current rising) induces a current in a facing coil Q in the **opposite** sense; opening the switch induces it in the **same** sense.

**Lenz is energy conservation.** If the induced current helped the change, a tiny push on a magnet would make it accelerate forever with current flowing — free energy. Instead you must do work against the opposing force, and that work becomes the electrical energy (and then heat).

sections.h: Motional emf: rods, rails and rotating rods
sections.md:
**Rod on rails.** A rod of length l moving with speed v perpendicular to B: **ε = Blv**. In terms of forces, each free charge feels qvB along the rod, so work per unit charge = vBl.

*Problem.* A 10 cm rod moves at 5 cm/s across a 0.4 T field... wait for the full picture: ε = 0.4 × 0.10 × 0.05 = **2 × 10⁻³ V**.

**Force and power.** If the circuit resistance is R, I = Blv/R and the field pushes back on the rod with F = BIl = B²l²v/R. To keep it at constant speed you must supply power P = Fv = **B²l²v²/R**, which appears as Joule heat I²R — energy is conserved.

*Problem.* l = 0.5 m, B = 0.2 T, v = 4 m/s, R = 1 Ω: ε = 0.4 V, I = 0.4 A, F = 0.2 × 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.04 N, P = 0.16 W = I²R ✓.

**Rotating rod.** A metal rod of length l rotating with angular speed ω about one end, perpendicular to B: the speed varies along the rod (v = ωr), so ε = ∫₀ˡ Bωr dr = **½Bωl²**.

*Problem.* A 1 m rod spins at 400 rad/s in 0.5 T: ε = ½ × 0.5 × 400 × 1 = **100 V** between centre and tip.

*Aeroplane wings.* A jet with 25 m wingspan flying horizontally at 250 m/s where the vertical component of Earth's field is 4 × 10⁻⁵ T: ε = 4 × 10⁻⁵ × 25 × 250 = **0.25 V** between wingtips — real, but harmless, since no closed circuit carries it.

sections.h: Eddy currents: induction in solid metal
sections.md:
When flux changes through a **solid** piece of metal, induced currents swirl inside it like eddies in a river. By Lenz's law they oppose the change — producing drag and heat.

**Seeing it.** A copper plate swinging between magnet poles comes to rest quickly. Cut slots in the plate and it swings much longer: the slots break up the current loops.

**Unwanted eddy currents** waste energy in transformer and motor cores. Cure: build cores from thin **laminated** sheets of iron insulated from each other, so the current paths are short and the resistance high.

**Useful eddy currents:**
- **Magnetic braking** in trains: strong electromagnets near the rails induce eddy currents that slow the train smoothly, without wear.
- **Electromagnetic damping** in moving-coil galvanometers: the coil is wound on a metal frame so the pointer settles quickly.
- **Induction furnaces and induction cooktops**: high-frequency alternating fields heat metal by eddy currents — the steel pan heats while the glass top stays relatively cool.
- **Electric power meters** (older analogue ones) use a rotating aluminium disc driven by eddy currents.

> **Did you know?** Drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe and it falls in slow motion — eddy currents in the pipe oppose its motion — even though copper is not attracted to magnets at all.

check.q: Transformer cores are laminated in order to:
check.why: Thin insulated sheets break up the circulating current paths, so much less energy is lost as heat.

sections.md:
**Mutual inductance** M: Φ₂ = MI₁ and ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt. For two long coaxial solenoids (inner radius r₁, length l, turns N₁ and N₂): **M = μ₀N₁N₂πr₁²/l** — the same whichever coil carries the current.

**Self-inductance** L: NΦ = LI and ε = −L dI/dt. For a long solenoid of n turns per metre, length l, area A: **L = μ₀n²Al**; with a core of relative permeability μ_r, multiply by μ_r.

*Problem.* A solenoid of 500 turns, length 0.5 m, area 4 × 10⁻⁴ m²: n = 1000 m⁻¹, L = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10⁶ × 4 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.5 ≈ **2.5 × 10⁻⁴ H**.

*Problem.* Current through a 5 mH coil rises at 200 A/s: back emf = 5 × 10⁻³ × 200 = **1 V**.

*Problem.* Current through a coil changes from 10 A to 2 A... uniformly in 0.1 s, inducing 4 V: L = 4 × 0.1/8 = **0.05 H**.

**Energy in an inductor:** building the current against the back emf stores **U = ½LI²** in the magnetic field — the inductor's version of ½CV². For L = 0.05 H and I = 10 A, U = 2.5 J. This is why switching off a large inductor can cause a spark: the stored energy has to go somewhere.

**Inductance as inertia.** Just as mass resists changes in velocity, inductance resists changes in current. ½LI² mirrors ½mv².

sections.md:
A coil of N turns and area A rotating at angular speed ω in field B has Φ = NBA cos ωt, so

**ε = NBAω sin ωt = ε₀ sin ωt**, with peak ε₀ = NBAω and ω = 2πν.

The emf is maximum when the plane of the coil is **parallel** to B (flux zero but changing fastest) and zero when the plane is perpendicular (flux maximum, momentarily not changing).

*Problem.* A 100-turn coil of area 0.1 m² rotates at 50 rev/s... let us use ν = 50 Hz, in B = 0.010 T. ε₀ = 100 × 0.010 × 0.1 × 2π × 50 = 0.1 × 314 ≈ **31.4 V**.

*Problem.* A coil of 72 turns, area 2.5 × 10⁻³ m², rotating at 50 rev/s... ν = 50 Hz in B = 3.0 × 10⁻² T: ε₀ = 72 × 0.03 × 2.5 × 10⁻³ × 314 ≈ **1.7 V**.

**Where the energy comes from.** In hydroelectric plants such as Bhakra Nangal, falling water turns the turbine; in thermal plants, steam does; in wind farms of Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, the wind. The generator itself only converts mechanical work into electrical energy — Lenz's law makes the coil hard to turn when current is drawn.

India's grid runs at **50 Hz**; the generators in big plants have many poles so that a slower shaft speed still gives 50 cycles per second.

check.q: The emf of an AC generator is maximum when the plane of the coil is:
check.why: With the plane parallel to B the flux is zero but changing at its fastest rate, so ε = NBAω sin ωt is at its peak.

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch07-alternating.title: Alternating Current
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch07-alternating.subtitle: Why your wall socket's 230 V actually swings to 325 V fifty times a second

sections.md:
In the 1880s, Thomas Edison championed direct current (DC) for city lighting. Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse backed alternating current (AC). AC won, for one decisive reason: its voltage can be stepped up and down easily with **transformers**, making long-distance transmission efficient. Today every grid in the world, including India's national grid, is AC.

An AC voltage varies sinusoidally:

v = v_m sin ωt

where v_m is the **peak value** and ω = 2πν the angular frequency. In India ν = 50 Hz; in the USA, 60 Hz.

In this chapter we analyse AC through a resistor, an inductor, a capacitor and their series combination, discover **resonance** (the principle of tuning a radio), understand **power factor**, and finish with the transformer.

check.q: The main reason AC is preferred for power distribution is that:
options: its voltage can be easily changed by transformers
check.why: Transformers let us transmit at very high voltage (low current, low I²R loss) and step down for use.

sections.h: 2. AC through a resistor; rms values
sections.md:
Apply v = v_m sin ωt to a resistor R. By Ohm's law i = (v_m/R) sin ωt = i_m sin ωt. Current and voltage are **in phase** — they peak together.

The average of a sine over a cycle is zero, so 'average current' is useless. But power i²R is always positive. Its average uses ⟨sin² ωt⟩ = ½:

P_avg = ½ i_m² R

We define the **root-mean-square (rms)** or **effective** current as the steady DC that gives the same heating:

I = i_m / √2 ≈ 0.707 i_m,  V = v_m / √2

Then P = I²R = VI, just like DC. All AC meters read rms values, and when we say 'mains is 230 V' we mean rms. The peak is 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V — which is why insulation must handle more than 230 V.

**Phasors.** A phasor is a rotating arrow of length v_m spinning anticlockwise at ω; its projection on the vertical axis gives v_m sin ωt. Phasors turn calculus into geometry: we add voltages by adding arrows.

sections.h: 3. AC through an inductor and a capacitor
sections.md:
**Pure inductor.** The source voltage equals L di/dt. Integrating, i = i_m sin(ωt − π/2) with i_m = v_m/(ωL). Current **lags** voltage by 90°. The opposition is the **inductive reactance**

X_L = ωL  (ohms)

X_L grows with frequency: an inductor blocks high frequencies and passes DC (X_L = 0 at ω = 0). Average power over a cycle is **zero** — energy is stored in the field for a quarter cycle and returned the next.

**Pure capacitor.** Charge q = Cv, so i = C dv/dt = i_m sin(ωt + π/2), with i_m = v_m ωC. Current **leads** voltage by 90°. **Capacitive reactance**

X_C = 1/(ωC)

falls with frequency: a capacitor blocks DC (X_C → ∞) and passes high frequencies. Average power again **zero**.

Memory aid: **ELI the ICE man** — in an inductor (L), E (voltage) comes before I; in a capacitor (C), I comes before E.
keyTerms: Inductive reactance X_L = ωL
Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/ωC
Lag/lead — phase difference between current and voltage

check.q: As the frequency of the AC source increases, the current through a pure capacitor:
check.why: X_C = 1/ωC falls as ω rises, so for fixed voltage the current increases.

sections.h: 4. The series LCR circuit and impedance
sections.md:
Connect R, L and C in series to v = v_m sin ωt. The same current flows through all. Phasors: V_R along I, V_L 90° ahead, V_C 90° behind. V_L and V_C point opposite, so they partly cancel. The resultant:

v_m² = V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²  ⇒  i_m = v_m / Z

with **impedance**

Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²]

and phase angle tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R, the angle by which voltage leads current.
- X_L > X_C: circuit is **inductive**, current lags voltage.
- X_C > X_L: circuit is **capacitive**, current leads.

The *impedance diagram* is a right triangle with sides R and (X_L − X_C) and hypotenuse Z.

check.q: In a series LCR circuit, R = 3 Ω, X_L = 8 Ω, X_C = 4 Ω. The impedance is:

sections.h: 5. Resonance — how a radio picks one station
sections.md:
Since X_L rises and X_C falls with ω, there's a frequency where they're equal. At this **resonant frequency**

ω₀ = 1/√(LC),  ν₀ = 1/(2π√(LC))

X_L = X_C, so Z = R (minimum) and the current is maximum, v_m/R, in phase with the voltage. The voltages across L and C can individually be much larger than the source voltage — they cancel each other.

Tuning an old radio turns a variable capacitor, shifting ω₀ until it matches a station's frequency. Only that station's signal drives a large current; others are ignored. (Resonance needs both L and C; an RL or RC circuit cannot resonate.)

**Sharpness — the Q-factor.** Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR). The **bandwidth** 2Δω = R/L is the range between frequencies where power drops to half. High Q (small R) means a sharp peak and better selectivity: Q = ω₀/(2Δω).

sections.h: 6. Power in AC circuits and the power factor
sections.md:
The instantaneous power p = vi. Averaging over a cycle for a series LCR circuit:

**P = V I cos φ**

where V and I are rms values and **cos φ** is the **power factor**.
- Pure resistor: φ = 0, cos φ = 1, P = VI.
- Pure L or C: φ = 90°, cos φ = 0, P = 0 — current flows but no average power is consumed. This is called **wattless current**.
- At resonance: cos φ = 1.

Also cos φ = R/Z.

**Why it matters.** Factories with many motors (inductive loads) have low power factors. To deliver the same useful power, they draw more current, which heats cables and transformers. Electricity boards in India penalise industrial consumers with low power factor; factories install **capacitor banks** to bring cos φ close to 1.

check.q: A circuit draws 5 A rms at 220 V rms with a phase angle of 60°. Average power is:

sections.md:
Charge a capacitor and connect it across an inductor (no resistance, no source). The capacitor discharges through L; current builds up and the energy moves into the magnetic field. When the capacitor is empty, the current keeps flowing (inductance is inertia) and charges the capacitor the opposite way. The cycle repeats:

q = q_m cos(ω₀ t),  ω₀ = 1/√(LC)

Energy sloshes between electric (q²/2C) and magnetic (½Li²) forms, with the total constant — exactly like a mass on a spring: L ↔ m, 1/C ↔ k, q ↔ x, i ↔ v.

Real circuits have resistance, so oscillations die out (damped) unless energy is fed in — which is what an electronic oscillator does.

check.q: In LC oscillations the electrical analogue of the mass on a spring is:
check.why: Inductance resists change in current the way mass resists change in velocity; the energy ½Li² matches ½mv².

sections.md:
A transformer has two coils — **primary** (N_p turns) and **secondary** (N_s turns) — wound on a laminated soft-iron core. AC in the primary creates changing flux that links the secondary. For an ideal transformer (no flux leakage, no losses, negligible primary resistance):

V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p,  I_s / I_p = N_p / N_s

so V_p I_p = V_s I_s (power in = power out).
- **Step-up** (N_s > N_p): raises voltage, lowers current — at power stations.
- **Step-down** (N_s < N_p): at substations and in phone chargers.

**Real losses:**
- *Flux leakage* — reduced by winding coils on top of each other.
- *Copper (I²R) loss* — thick wires.
- *Eddy currents* in the core — laminated core.
- *Hysteresis* — soft iron with a narrow loop.

Large transformers are 95–99% efficient. A typical chain: generated at ~11–25 kV, stepped up to 220–765 kV for transmission, then stepped down in stages to 11 kV and finally 230 V for your home.

rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch07-alternating.title: Alternating Current — Part 2: Phasors, Problems and the Power Grid
rd-school-c12-physics-a.ch07-alternating.subtitle: Phasor diagrams, reactance, LCR resonance, sharpness, power factor and transformers — every exercise type worked out

sections.md:
Part 1 covered the chapter's sections: the AC–DC story, AC in a resistor and rms values, AC in an inductor and a capacitor, the series LCR circuit and impedance, resonance, power and power factor, LC oscillations and the transformer.

This part gives you the **phasor method** properly, then solves the standard numericals of every section, and ends with the transformer's real-world losses and India's grid.

Key symbols: v = v_m sin ωt, ω = 2πν; India's mains is **230 V rms at 50 Hz**, so the peak voltage is 230√2 ≈ 325 V.

> **Did you know?** The voltage at your wall socket reverses direction 100 times every second (50 full cycles). A filament bulb's brightness flickers at 100 Hz, but your eyes cannot follow it.

sections.h: Phasors: spinning arrows that do the trigonometry
sections.md:
A **phasor** is an arrow of length equal to the peak value, rotating anticlockwise at angular speed ω. Its projection on the vertical axis gives the instantaneous value. Two quantities with a phase difference are two arrows at a fixed angle, spinning together.

| Element | Phase of current relative to voltage | Opposition |
|---|---|---|
| Resistor R | in phase | R |
| Inductor L | current **lags** by π/2 | X_L = ωL |
| Capacitor C | current **leads** by π/2 | X_C = 1/(ωC) |

Memory aid: **ELI the ICE man** — in L, E (voltage) comes before I; in C, I comes before E.

**Series LCR with phasors.** The same current i flows through all three. Draw I horizontally. V_R is along I, V_L points up (ahead by 90°), V_C points down. The net reactive voltage is V_L − V_C, and

V² = V_R² + (V_L − V_C)² ⇒ **Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²)**, **tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R**.

If X_L > X_C the circuit is **inductive** (current lags); if X_C > X_L it is **capacitive** (current leads).

sections.md:
**Resistor.** A 100 Ω resistor on 220 V, 50 Hz: I_rms = 2.2 A; peak current 2.2√2 ≈ 3.11 A; average power = V_rmsI_rms = **484 W**.

**Inductor.** A 44 mH inductor on 220 V, 50 Hz: X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.044 ≈ 13.8 Ω; I_rms = 220/13.8 ≈ **15.9 A**. Average power **0** — energy flows in and out each cycle.

**Capacitor.** A 60 μF capacitor on 110 V, 60 Hz: X_C = 1/(2π × 60 × 60 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 44.2 Ω; I_rms = 110/44.2 ≈ **2.49 A**; average power 0.

**How reactance depends on frequency.** X_L = ωL rises with frequency — an inductor blocks high frequencies and passes DC (ω = 0 ⇒ X_L = 0). X_C = 1/(ωC) falls with frequency — a capacitor blocks DC (infinite reactance) and passes high frequencies. This is the basis of the tone controls and crossover filters in speakers.

**Choke coil.** To dim a tube light or limit current without wasting power, use an inductor (choke) rather than a resistor: its average power is nearly zero, while a resistor would get hot.

check.q: As the frequency of an AC supply increases, the reactance of a capacitor:
check.why: X_C = 1/(2πνC) is inversely proportional to frequency.

sections.md:
*Problem.* R = 200 Ω, C = 15 μF, L not present (an RC circuit) on 220 V, 50 Hz. X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 15 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 212 Ω. Z = √(200² + 212²) ≈ 291.5 Ω. I = 220/291.5 ≈ **0.755 A**. V_R = 151 V, V_C = 160 V; their arithmetic sum (311 V) exceeds 220 V, but the **phasor** sum √(151² + 160²) ≈ 220 V ✓. Never add rms voltages of different elements directly.

**Resonance.** When X_L = X_C, Z = R (minimum), current is maximum and in phase with the voltage:

**ω₀ = 1/√(LC)**, ν₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).

*Problem.* L = 5.0 H, C = 80 μF, R = 40 Ω on a variable-frequency 230 V source. ω₀ = 1/√(5 × 80 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/√(4 × 10⁻⁴) = **50 rad/s** (ν₀ ≈ 8 Hz). At resonance I_rms = 230/40 = **5.75 A**, I_peak ≈ 8.13 A. Voltage across L: I X_L = 5.75 × (50 × 5) = **1437.5 V** — far greater than the source voltage! V_C is the same and opposite, so they cancel. (This is why resonance circuits need well-insulated parts.)

**Sharpness and Q-factor.** Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR). Bandwidth 2Δω = R/L. Higher Q ⇒ narrower, sharper peak ⇒ better tuning. For the problem above, Q = 50 × 5/40 = **6.25**.

**Tuning a radio.** Turning the dial changes C; the circuit resonates with one station's frequency, which produces a large current, while others produce tiny ones. Resonance needs both L and C — an RL or RC circuit cannot resonate.

sections.md:
Average power **P = V_rms I_rms cos φ**; cos φ = R/Z is the **power factor**.

| Circuit | φ | cos φ | Power |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure R | 0 | 1 | maximum |
| Pure L or pure C | ±π/2 | 0 | zero (**wattless current**) |
| LCR at resonance | 0 | 1 | maximum |

**Wattless current.** The component I sin φ of the current is out of phase with the voltage and delivers no average power, though it still flows and heats the wires.

*Problem.* An LCR circuit with R = 3 Ω, X_L = 25 Ω, X_C = 21 Ω on 220 V: Z = √(9 + 16) = 5 Ω, I = 44 A, cos φ = 3/5 = 0.6, P = 220 × 44 × 0.6 = **5808 W** (= I²R = 1936 × 3 ✓).

**Why industry cares.** Factories with big motors draw inductive current, lowering cos φ. For the same useful power, a low power factor means more current, more I²R loss in transmission lines, and bigger cables. Electricity boards charge penalties for low power factor, so factories add **capacitor banks** to bring cos φ close to 1.

check.q: A circuit has R = 3 Ω and Z = 5 Ω. Its power factor is:
check.why: Power factor cos φ = R/Z = 3/5 = 0.6.

sections.h: LC oscillations and the mechanical analogy
sections.md:
A charged capacitor connected to an inductor makes charge slosh back and forth: q = q_m cos ω₀t with **ω₀ = 1/√(LC)**. Energy swaps between the electric field (q²/2C) and the magnetic field (½Li²); the total stays q_m²/2C if there is no resistance.

| Mass on spring | LC circuit |
|---|---|
| displacement x | charge q |
| velocity v | current i |
| mass m | inductance L |
| spring constant k | 1/C |
| ½mv² | ½Li² |
| ½kx² | q²/2C |
| ω = √(k/m) | ω = 1/√(LC) |

*Problem.* A 30 μF capacitor charged to 6 mC is connected to a 27 mH inductor. ω₀ = 1/√(27 × 10⁻³ × 30 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/√(8.1 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 1.11 × 10³ rad/s, so ν ≈ **177 Hz**. Total energy = q²/2C = (6 × 10⁻³)²/(6 × 10⁻⁵) = **0.6 J**.

In real circuits resistance drains energy as heat and radiation, so the oscillations die away — just as friction stops a pendulum.

check.q: In the LC–spring analogy, inductance L corresponds to:
check.why: Inductance resists changes in current just as mass resists changes in velocity, and ½Li² mirrors ½mv².

sections.md:
For an ideal transformer: **V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p = I_p/I_s**. Step-up: N_s > N_p; step-down: N_s < N_p. Power in = power out (ideal).

*Problem.* A step-down transformer converts 2300 V to 230 V: turns ratio 10 : 1. If the secondary supplies 4.6 kW, I_s = 20 A and I_p = 2 A.

**Real-world losses and cures:**
- **Flux leakage** — not all primary flux links the secondary; wind coils over each other.
- **Copper (I²R) loss** in windings — use thick wire for the high-current side.
- **Eddy currents** in the core — laminate it.
- **Hysteresis loss** — use soft iron with a thin hysteresis loop.

**Why high-voltage transmission?** Power station generators produce around 11 kV; step-up transformers raise it to 220 kV or 400 kV (some Indian lines use 765 kV). For the same power, current falls, so line losses I²R fall by the square. Near cities, sub-stations step it down to 33 kV, 11 kV and finally a pole transformer gives **230 V** to homes.

*Problem.* A town needs 800 kW at 220 V. With a line resistance of 15 Ω and transmission at 4000 V, I = 200 A, loss = 200² × 15 = **600 kW** — a huge fraction! At 40 000 V the current is 20 A and the loss only 6 kW. That single comparison explains the whole grid.

check.q: Transmitting the same power at 10 times the voltage reduces line loss by a factor of:
check.why: Current falls by 10, and loss I²R falls by 10² = 100.

rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch08-electromagn.title: Electromagnetic Waves
rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch08-electromagn.subtitle: One missing term in Maxwell's equations — and suddenly light, radio and X-rays are the same thing

sections.md:
Your phone right now is bathed in invisible waves: 4G and 5G signals, Wi-Fi, FM radio, GPS from satellites 20,000 km above, and the warm infrared glow of your own body. Every one of them is the same kind of thing as the light from the screen: an **electromagnetic wave**. This chapter shows where these waves come from.

The story begins with a puzzle. Ampere's law says ∮B·dl = μ₀ i. Charge a capacitor through a wire and apply the law to a small loop around the wire: the current i passes through a flat surface bounded by the loop, so B ≠ 0. But now take a balloon-shaped surface bounded by the *same* loop that bulges out between the capacitor plates. No conduction current crosses it — so the law gives B = 0. The same loop cannot have two different fields. Something is missing.

James Clerk Maxwell (around 1864) found it. Between the plates, the *electric flux* is changing as the capacitor charges. He proposed that a changing electric field acts like a current — the **displacement current**:

i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E / dt

The corrected **Ampere–Maxwell law** is

∮ B · dl = μ₀ (i_c + ε₀ dΦ_E/dt)

On the flat surface, i_c flows; on the balloon surface, i_d flows; and the two are exactly equal. The paradox vanishes.
keyTerms: Displacement current — ε₀ dΦ_E/dt, the 'current' due to a changing electric field
Ampere–Maxwell law — magnetic fields are produced by conduction and displacement currents

check.q: Displacement current exists wherever there is:
check.why: i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt is non-zero only when the electric flux changes with time.

sections.h: 2. Maxwell's equations and the prediction of light
sections.md:
With the correction, the four laws of electromagnetism are complete and symmetric:

1. **Gauss's law (electric):** ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀
2. **Gauss's law (magnetic):** ∮B·dA = 0
3. **Faraday's law:** ∮E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt — a changing B makes E.
4. **Ampere–Maxwell law:** ∮B·dl = μ₀i_c + μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt — a changing E makes B.

Laws 3 and 4 together mean a disturbance can feed itself: changing E creates changing B, which creates changing E… and the pair travels through empty space. Maxwell calculated the speed:

**c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀)**

Plug in μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²): c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s — exactly the measured speed of light! Maxwell concluded that light *is* an electromagnetic wave. Electricity, magnetism and optics became one subject.

In 1887 Heinrich Hertz generated and detected such waves in the lab using sparks. In the 1890s **Jagadish Chandra Bose** in Kolkata produced and studied very short (millimetre-range, 5 mm to 25 mm) waves and built detectors, and Guglielmo Marconi transmitted radio signals over long distances.

check.q: Maxwell's equations predict the speed of EM waves in vacuum to be:
check.why: The wave equation from Faraday's and Ampere–Maxwell's laws gives c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

sections.md:
A stationary charge makes only an electric field. A charge moving at constant velocity makes steady E and B fields. Neither radiates. **An accelerated charge** produces changing E and B fields that break away and travel outward — that is radiation.

The simplest source: a charge oscillating with frequency ν. Its oscillating fields create a wave of the same frequency. That is exactly what a radio antenna does: an AC current makes electrons accelerate back and forth along a metal rod.

For visible light, the 'oscillators' are electrons in atoms making transitions between energy levels (Chapter 12). For X-rays, fast electrons decelerating suddenly in a metal target.

check.q: Electromagnetic waves are produced by:
check.why: Only accelerating charges create the time-varying fields that radiate away as EM waves.

sections.md:
For a wave travelling along z:

E_x = E₀ sin(kz − ωt),  B_y = B₀ sin(kz − ωt)

Key properties:
- E, B and the direction of propagation are **mutually perpendicular**; the wave travels along E × B. EM waves are **transverse**.
- E and B oscillate **in phase**.
- **E₀ / B₀ = c** in vacuum. (If E₀ = 300 V/m, B₀ = 10⁻⁶ T — the magnetic part looks tiny but carries equal energy.)
- k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πν, and c = νλ = ω/k.
- No medium is needed; they travel through vacuum.
- In a material medium the speed is v = 1/√(με) = c/n, where n is the refractive index.
- They carry **energy** and **momentum**. If a wave delivers energy U to a surface and is fully absorbed, it transfers momentum p = U/c. This is **radiation pressure** — tiny for sunlight (a few micropascals) but enough to push 'solar sails' on spacecraft.
- Energy density is shared equally: u_E = ½ε₀E² equals u_B = B²/(2μ₀).

sections.md:
All EM waves are alike except for wavelength (and so frequency). Arranged in order:

| Band | Wavelength (approx.) | Produced by | Uses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Radio | > 0.1 m | accelerating charges in antennas | AM/FM, TV, mobile (≈ 0.8–3 GHz and beyond) |
| Microwaves | 0.1 m – 1 mm | klystrons, magnetrons, Gunn diodes | radar, microwave ovens (≈ 2.45 GHz), satellite links |
| Infrared | 1 mm – 700 nm | hot bodies, molecular vibrations | remote controls, night vision, physiotherapy, greenhouse effect |
| Visible | 700 – 400 nm | electron transitions in atoms | sight, photography, photosynthesis |
| Ultraviolet | 400 nm – 1 nm | very hot bodies like the Sun; special lamps | water purification, LASIK eye surgery, detecting forged notes |
| X-rays | 1 nm – 10⁻³ nm | fast electrons hitting metal targets | medical imaging, cancer therapy, crystallography |
| Gamma rays | < 10⁻³ nm | nuclear reactions, radioactive decay | cancer treatment, sterilising equipment |

Visible light is a thin slice: about 400–700 nm. Our eyes are most sensitive near 550 nm (yellow-green) — close to where sunlight is brightest.

**Ozone and UV.** The ozone layer absorbs most harmful UV from the Sun; ordinary glass also absorbs much UV, which is why you don't get sunburnt through a window.

**Microwave ovens** work because the microwave frequency matches a rotational/vibrational response of water molecules, which absorb energy and heat the food.

parts.md: Kolkata, the 1890s. In a public demonstration that is still told in physics classrooms, Jagadish Chandra Bose is said to have sent invisible waves through walls to trigger a distant device — a bell rang, gunpowder fired. Accounts of the exact details vary, but his research papers are well documented: he generated waves of a few millimetres to a few centimetres, built horn antennas, waveguides and an improved 'coherer' detector, and studied their reflection, refraction and polarisation — showing these invisible waves behaved exactly as Maxwell predicted light should.

Bose chose not to patent most of his work, believing science should be shared freely. Decades later, the millimetre waves he explored became central to radar, radio astronomy and today's 5G networks. When your phone locks onto a high-band 5G signal in a Bengaluru mall, it is using a region of the spectrum a Kolkata physicist was mapping more than a century ago with home-built equipment.

rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch08-electromagn.title: Electromagnetic Waves — Part 2: Displacement Current, Wave Numbers and a Tour of the Spectrum
rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch08-electromagn.subtitle: From a charging capacitor to the Wi-Fi in your home — every exercise type and every band explained

sections.md:
Part 1 followed the chapter: the puzzle of the capacitor that led Maxwell to the **displacement current**, Maxwell's equations and the prediction that light is an electromagnetic wave, how accelerated charges produce EM waves, the nature of the waves, and the electromagnetic spectrum.

Part 2 goes deeper on each, with numbers:

1. Displacement current — a numerical treatment.
2. The wave equations E = E₀ sin(kz − ωt), B = B₀ sin(kz − ωt) and how to read them.
3. Energy, intensity and **radiation pressure**.
4. A band-by-band tour of the spectrum: sources, detectors, uses and safety.
5. Exercise drills.

> **Did you know?** Jagadish Chandra Bose generated and detected microwaves of wavelength from about 25 mm down to 5 mm in Kolkata in the 1890s, and demonstrated them publicly — among the earliest millimetre-wave experiments anywhere.

Ampere's law ∮B · dl = μ₀I fails for a charging capacitor: a loop round the wire encloses current, but a surface bulging through the gap encloses none. Maxwell fixed it by adding the **displacement current**

**I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt**,

so that ∮B · dl = μ₀(I_c + I_d) — the Ampere–Maxwell law. Inside the gap I_d exactly equals the conduction current in the wires, so current is 'continuous'.

*Problem.* A parallel-plate capacitor with circular plates of radius 12 cm, separation 5 mm, is charged by a 0.15 A current... For a capacitor with plate area A, E = q/(ε₀A), so Φ_E = EA = q/ε₀ and I_d = ε₀ d(q/ε₀)/dt = dq/dt = I. Hence the displacement current between the plates is **0.15 A**, equal to the charging current.

*Rate of change of field.* The same capacitor: dE/dt = I/(ε₀A) = 0.15/(8.85 × 10⁻¹² × π × 0.0144) = 0.15/(4.0 × 10⁻¹³) ≈ **3.7 × 10¹¹ V m⁻¹ s⁻¹**. A huge rate, yet a modest current.

*Magnetic field in the gap.* At a distance r from the axis inside the plates, only the fraction r²/R² of I_d is enclosed: B = μ₀I_d r/(2πR²). At the plate edge (r = R) B = μ₀I/(2πR), the same as near a straight wire.

**Why it matters.** The displacement-current term means a changing electric field makes a magnetic field — the mirror of Faraday's law. Each regenerates the other, and the pair can travel through empty space: an electromagnetic wave.

check.q: The displacement current between the plates of a capacitor being charged by current I is:
check.why: I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = dq/dt, exactly the charging current, so current is continuous through the gap.

sections.md:
A plane EM wave travelling along +z:

E_x = E₀ sin(kz − ωt), B_y = B₀ sin(kz − ωt).

- **k = 2π/λ** is the wave number; **ω = 2πν**.
- Speed **c = ω/k = νλ = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s** in vacuum.
- **E₀/B₀ = c**.
- E, B and the direction of travel are mutually perpendicular: the wave travels along **E × B**. EM waves are **transverse**.
- E and B are **in phase** — both peak together.
- In a medium, v = 1/√(με) and the refractive index n = c/v = √(μ_rε_r).

*Problem.* A plane wave of frequency 25 MHz travels in vacuum along x. At a point, E = 6.3 ĵ V/m. Then B = E/c = 6.3/(3 × 10⁸) = **2.1 × 10⁻⁸ T**, along ẑ (since x̂ is the direction of E × B: ĵ × k̂ = î ✓).

*Problem.* The magnetic field of a wave is B_y = 2 × 10⁻⁷ sin(0.5 × 10³ x + 1.5 × 10¹¹ t) T. Then k = 500 m⁻¹ ⇒ λ = 2π/500 ≈ **1.26 cm**; ω = 1.5 × 10¹¹ ⇒ ν ≈ **23.9 GHz** (microwave). E₀ = cB₀ = **60 V/m**. The '+' sign shows it travels along **−x**.

*Check:* ω/k = 1.5 × 10¹¹/500 = 3 × 10⁸ m/s ✓.

sections.md:
EM waves carry energy. The average energy density is shared equally between the fields: u_avg = ½ε₀E₀² (half electric, half magnetic, since ε₀E²/2 = B²/2μ₀ when E = cB).

**Intensity** (power per unit area) I = u_avg c = ½ε₀cE₀².

They also carry **momentum**. If energy U is completely absorbed by a surface, the momentum delivered is **p = U/c**; if it is perfectly reflected, 2U/c. This gives a **radiation pressure** I/c (absorbed).

*Problem.* Sunlight at Earth has intensity about 1.4 kW/m². Radiation pressure on an absorbing surface = 1400/(3 × 10⁸) ≈ **4.7 × 10⁻⁶ Pa** — tiny, but enough to push a large thin **solar sail** in space. Peak field: E₀ = √(2I/(ε₀c)) = √(2800/(8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 3 × 10⁸)) = √(1.05 × 10⁶) ≈ **1.0 × 10³ V/m**.

*Problem.* A 100 W bulb converts about 5% to visible light. At 1 m (spreading over 4πr²): I = 5/(4π) ≈ 0.40 W/m². At 10 m: 0.004 W/m² — the inverse-square law.

*Problem.* The heating of your hands near a fire, or the warmth of the Sun on your face in a Delhi winter, is EM energy (mostly infrared) being absorbed.

check.q: Radiation of energy U is fully reflected by a mirror at normal incidence. Momentum delivered:
check.why: The momentum reverses direction, so the change is 2U/c.

sections.md:
All EM waves travel at c in vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength. In order of **increasing frequency** (decreasing wavelength):

| Band | Approx. wavelength | Produced by | Detected by | Uses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Radio | > 0.1 m | oscillating charges in antennas | receiver aerials | AM/FM radio, TV, mobile phones (~1–2 GHz in part are microwaves) |
| Microwave | 0.1 m – 1 mm | klystrons, magnetrons, Gunn diodes | point-contact diodes | radar, satellite links, ovens (2.45 GHz), Wi-Fi |
| Infrared | 1 mm – 700 nm | hot bodies, molecular vibrations | thermopiles, bolometers, IR film | remote controls, night vision, physiotherapy, greenhouse effect |
| Visible | 700 – 400 nm | electrons in atoms changing levels | eye, photocells, film | sight, photography, optical fibres |
| Ultraviolet | 400 nm – 1 nm | very hot bodies (Sun), arc lamps | photocells, film | sterilising water, LASIK eye surgery, detecting fake notes |
| X-rays | 1 nm – 10⁻³ nm | electrons hitting metal targets | film, Geiger tubes | medical imaging, airport security, crystal structure |
| Gamma rays | < 10⁻³ nm | radioactive nuclei | Geiger tubes, ionisation chambers | cancer therapy, sterilising instruments, astronomy |

(Band edges overlap; the classification is by source as much as by wavelength.)

**Safety notes.** The **ozone layer** absorbs most solar UV; its thinning raises skin-cancer risk. X-rays and gamma rays are **ionising** — medical use is carefully limited. **Infrared** from the Sun warms Earth's surface; greenhouse gases trap the IR that Earth re-emits.

**The eye's window.** Our eyes respond to about 400–700 nm, peaking near 550 nm (yellow-green) — close to the peak of sunlight. Bees see some UV; snakes like pit vipers sense IR.

check.why: Remote controls use infrared LEDs, invisible to the eye but easily detected by a photodiode in the TV.

sections.md:
**1. Frequency to wavelength.** FM radio at 98.3 MHz: λ = c/ν = 3 × 10⁸/9.83 × 10⁷ ≈ **3.05 m**. A microwave oven at 2.45 GHz: λ ≈ **12.2 cm**.

**2. Photon energy (links to Chapter 11).** E = hν. For visible light of 500 nm: ν = 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz, E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 6 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ **2.5 eV**. X-ray photons are thousands of eV; radio photons are about 10⁻⁷ eV — which is why X-rays can ionise atoms and radio waves cannot.

**3. Which band?** A wave of λ = 10 nm is ultraviolet (near X-rays); 1 μm is infrared; 1 cm is microwave.

**4. LC circuit as a source.** An LC circuit with L = 1 μH and C = 100 pF oscillates at ν = 1/(2π√(10⁻⁶ × 10⁻¹⁰)) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁸) ≈ **15.9 MHz** — a radio wave of λ ≈ 19 m.

**5. Speed in a medium.** Glass with ε_r ≈ 2.25 and μ_r ≈ 1: n = 1.5, v = 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Frequency stays the same entering the glass; wavelength shrinks by 1.5.

**6. Conceptual.** Why are EM waves not deflected by electric or magnetic fields? They carry no charge. Why can sound not travel through vacuum, while light can? Sound needs a medium; EM fields regenerate each other with no medium.

rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch09-ray-optics.title: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch09-ray-optics.subtitle: Mirrors, mirages, rainbows and telescopes — all from two simple rules about straight lines

sections.md:
Drive along a Rajasthan highway at noon and you'll see 'water' shimmering on the road ahead that vanishes as you approach. Look at a pencil in a glass of water and it appears broken. Look through a diamond and it sparkles far more than glass. All of this is **ray optics**.

Light is an electromagnetic wave (Chapter 8) with wavelength 400–700 nm. When objects and openings are much larger than this, we can ignore wave effects and treat light as travelling in straight lines called **rays**. Two rules then explain almost everything:

1. **Reflection:** angle of incidence = angle of reflection, and incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
2. **Refraction (Snell's law):** n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.

**Sign convention (Cartesian, used by NCERT):** measure all distances from the pole (mirror) or optical centre (lens). Distances in the direction of incident light are positive; against it, negative. Heights above the principal axis are positive, below negative. Usually light is drawn from left to right, so the object distance u is negative.

check.q: Ray optics is a valid approximation when:
options: wavelength is much larger than obstacles
wavelength is much smaller than obstacles
check.why: When objects are much larger than the wavelength, diffraction is negligible and light travels in straight lines.

sections.md:
A spherical mirror is part of a sphere of radius R (the **radius of curvature**). For rays close to the axis (paraxial rays), parallel rays meet (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) the **principal focus** F, with

**f = R/2**

The **mirror equation**:

1/v + 1/u = 1/f

and **magnification** m = h′/h = −v/u.

With the sign convention, a concave mirror has f negative, a convex mirror f positive. A negative m means an inverted (real) image; positive m an erect (virtual) image.

**Concave mirror image positions:** object beyond C → real, inverted, diminished, between F and C; at C → at C, same size; between C and F → beyond C, magnified; at F → at infinity; between F and P → virtual, erect, magnified behind the mirror (used in shaving and dentists' mirrors).

**Convex mirror:** always virtual, erect, diminished — wide field of view, hence used as rear-view mirrors ('objects in mirror are closer than they appear').

sections.h: 3. Refraction, apparent depth and total internal reflection
sections.md:
When light enters a medium of different refractive index, it bends. **Refractive index** n = c/v. The relative index n₂₁ = n₂/n₁. Light bends **toward the normal** entering a denser medium.

**Apparent depth.** A coin at real depth h in water (n = 1.33) seems to be at h/n — it looks raised. A swimming pool appears shallower than it is, which is why it's dangerous to judge depth by eye.

**Total internal reflection (TIR).** Going from denser to rarer medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the **critical angle** i_c, the refracted ray grazes the surface (r = 90°):

sin i_c = n₂/n₁ (= 1/n for medium-to-air)

For i > i_c, *all* light reflects back. Critical angles: water ~49°, glass ~42°, diamond ~24°.

Applications:
- **Mirage:** on a hot road, air near the surface is hotter and rarer. Light from the sky bends gradually and undergoes TIR, reaching your eye from below — you 'see' the sky as a pool on the road.
- **Diamond's sparkle:** low critical angle; cutters shape facets so light undergoes many TIRs inside.
- **Prisms** turning light by 90° or 180° in periscopes and binoculars.
- **Optical fibres:** glass cores with a cladding of lower n; light zig-zags by TIR for kilometres. India's BharatNet project uses optical fibre to bring broadband to villages.

sections.h: 4. Refraction at spherical surfaces and thin lenses
sections.md:
For a spherical surface of radius R separating media n₁ (object side) and n₂:

n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R

Apply this twice — once for each face of a thin lens — and you get the **lens maker's formula**:

1/f = (n₂₁ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)

where n₂₁ is the lens's index relative to the surrounding medium. A biconvex lens has R₁ > 0, R₂ < 0 (f positive, converging). Note: a convex glass lens in a liquid of higher index becomes diverging!

The **thin lens formula**:

1/v − 1/u = 1/f,  m = v/u

**Power** P = 1/f (f in metres), unit **dioptre (D)**. Converging lenses have positive power. Your optometrist's prescription of '−2.0' means a diverging lens of f = −50 cm.

**Lenses in contact:** powers add, P = P₁ + P₂ + …, i.e., 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂. Total magnification of a multi-lens system is the product m = m₁m₂m₃….

sections.md:
A ray passing through a triangular prism of angle A bends twice. The total **angle of deviation** δ = i + e − A, with r₁ + r₂ = A.

As you increase the angle of incidence, δ first decreases, reaches a minimum **δ_m**, then increases. At minimum deviation, the ray passes symmetrically: i = e and r₁ = r₂ = A/2. Then

n = sin[(A + δ_m)/2] / sin(A/2)

This is how we measure refractive index in the lab. For a **thin prism** (small A), δ ≈ (n − 1)A.

*(Dispersion — the splitting of white light into colours because n depends on wavelength, violet bending most — and natural phenomena like the rainbow and blue sky appeared in older editions; they're still lovely to know: a primary rainbow forms by one internal reflection in raindrops and appears at about 40–42° from the antisolar point.)*

check.q: At minimum deviation in an equilateral prism, the angle of refraction r inside the prism is:
check.why: At minimum deviation r₁ = r₂ = A/2 = 30°.

sections.md:
**The eye** has a near point of about **D = 25 cm** for normal vision — the closest distance at which you can see clearly. An object's apparent size depends on the angle it makes at the eye.

**Simple microscope (magnifier):** a convex lens held close to the eye. With the image at the near point:

m = 1 + D/f

With the image at infinity (relaxed eye): m = D/f. A jeweller's loupe with f = 5 cm gives about 5–6×.

**Compound microscope:** a short-focus **objective** forms a real, magnified image; the **eyepiece** magnifies that image further. Total magnification

m = m_o × m_e ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e)  (final image at infinity)

where L is the **tube length** (distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece). Short focal lengths for both lenses give high magnification. School microscopes reach about 400×.

check.q: A simple microscope with f = 5 cm, image at the near point (25 cm), gives magnification:

sections.md:
**Refracting telescope:** a long-focus objective (f_o) forms a real image of a distant object at its focus; the eyepiece (f_e) magnifies it. In normal adjustment (final image at infinity):

m = f_o / f_e,  length L = f_o + f_e

A larger objective collects more light (better for faint stars) and resolves finer detail.

**Reflecting telescopes** use a concave mirror as the objective. Advantages: no chromatic aberration (mirrors reflect all colours the same), spherical aberration removed with a parabolic mirror, and a mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made much larger than a lens. The **Cassegrain** design uses a small convex secondary mirror to send light through a hole in the primary.

India's largest optical telescopes include the 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope near Nainital (Uttarakhand), a reflector. The world's giants, with mirrors of 8–10 m and more, are all reflectors.

rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch09-ray-optics-.title: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments — Part 2: The Sign Convention and Every Numerical Type
rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch09-ray-optics-.subtitle: Mirrors, slabs, fibres, lens-maker's formula, combinations, prisms, the eye and instruments — worked from first principles

sections.h: The Cartesian sign convention — get this right first
sections.md:
Part 1 walked through the chapter: rays, spherical mirrors, refraction with apparent depth and total internal reflection, refraction at spherical surfaces and thin lenses, the prism, the microscope and telescopes.

Nearly every wrong answer in this chapter is a sign error. Use the **Cartesian sign convention** without exception:

1. All distances are measured **from the pole** (mirror) or **optical centre** (lens).
2. Distances in the direction of the **incident light** are **positive**; against it, **negative**. (Light is drawn travelling left to right, so the object is usually at negative u.)
3. Heights **above** the principal axis are positive, below negative.

Consequences: a concave mirror has f < 0; a convex mirror f > 0; a convex lens f > 0; a concave lens f < 0. A real image formed by a mirror has v < 0; a real image by a lens has v > 0.

**Formulas:**
- Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, m = −v/u, f = R/2.
- Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u.
- Power P = 1/f (f in metres), unit dioptre (D).

> **Did you know?** Ibn al-Haytham's *Book of Optics* (around 1020 CE) argued that we see because light enters the eye from objects — not, as many earlier thinkers held, because the eye sends out rays.

*Concave mirror, real image.* Object 27 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius 36 cm (f = −18 cm). 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/18 + 1/27 = (−3 + 2)/54 = −1/54 ⇒ **v = −54 cm** (real, in front). m = −v/u = −(−54)/(−27) = **−2**: inverted, twice the size.

*Same mirror, object at 9 cm (inside f).* 1/v = −1/18 + 1/9 = 1/18 ⇒ **v = +18 cm** (behind the mirror, virtual). m = −18/(−9) = **+2**: erect and magnified — a shaving or make-up mirror.

*Convex mirror.* A car's rear-view mirror has R = 2 m (f = +1 m). A bus 6 m behind (u = −6 m): 1/v = 1 + 1/6 = 7/6 ⇒ v = +6/7 m ≈ 0.86 m; m = −(6/7)/(−6) = **+1/7**. The image is virtual, erect and small, so a wide field of view fits in a small mirror — which is why such mirrors carry the warning that objects are closer than they appear.

*Moving object.* If an object moves towards a concave mirror from far away to F, the real image moves from F out to infinity, growing all the way.

check.q: An object is 9 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 18 cm. The image is:
check.why: With u = −9 and f = −18, v = +18 cm (behind the mirror) and m = +2 — virtual, erect and magnified.

sections.h: Refraction: slabs, apparent depth and fibres
sections.md:
**Snell's law:** n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r. Refractive index n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂.

**Glass slab.** The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but **laterally shifted**; the shift grows with thickness and angle of incidence.

**Apparent depth.** Viewed from directly above, an object at real depth d in a liquid of index n appears at **d/n**. A coin at the bottom of a 15 cm bucket of water (n = 1.33) appears about 11.3 cm deep — raised by 3.7 cm. A swimming pool always looks shallower than it is, which is why lifeguards warn people.

*Problem.* A microscope focused on a mark is raised by 1.0 cm to refocus after a 3.0 cm glass slab (n = 1.5) is placed over it? Shift = t(1 − 1/n) = 3(1 − 2/3) = **1.0 cm** ✓.

**Total internal reflection (TIR)** happens when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle C, where **sin C = n_rarer/n_denser**. Glass–air (n = 1.5): C ≈ 41.8°. Water–air: C ≈ 48.8°. Diamond (n = 2.42): C ≈ 24.4° — so light bounces many times inside a cut diamond, making it sparkle.

**Everyday TIR:**
- **Mirages** on hot roads in Rajasthan: hot air near the ground is less dense, light from the sky bends and is totally reflected upward, looking like water.
- **Totally reflecting prisms** (45°–90°–45°) turn rays by 90° or 180° in periscopes and binoculars.
- **Optical fibres**: a glass core (n ≈ 1.68) surrounded by cladding (n ≈ 1.44) traps light by repeated TIR, carrying internet data across India and enabling endoscopy.

**Sunrise trick.** Atmospheric refraction lets us see the Sun about 2 minutes before it actually rises above the horizon and 2 minutes after it sets.

sections.h: Spherical surfaces and the lens-maker's formula
sections.md:
**Single refracting surface** (from medium n₁ into n₂, radius R): **n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R**.

*Problem.* A small bulb is 7.5 cm deep under the curved surface... take a simpler case: an object in air 30 cm from a convex glass surface (n = 1.5, R = +20 cm). 1.5/v − 1/(−30) = 0.5/20 ⇒ 1.5/v = 1/40 − 1/30 = −1/120 ⇒ v = −180 cm. The image is virtual, 180 cm in front of the surface on the object's side.

**Lens-maker's formula** (thin lens of index n in air): **1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)**.

*Problem.* A double-convex lens with R₁ = +10 cm, R₂ = −15 cm, n = 1.5: 1/f = 0.5(1/10 + 1/15) = 0.5 × (5/30) = 1/12 ⇒ **f = 12 cm**.

*Problem.* A plano-convex lens (R₁ = ∞... curved side first: R₁ = +20 cm, R₂ = ∞) with n = 1.5: 1/f = 0.5/20 ⇒ f = 40 cm.

**A lens in a liquid.** In a medium of index n_m, replace (n − 1) by (n/n_m − 1). A glass lens (n = 1.5) in water (1.33): factor 0.128 instead of 0.5, so f becomes about 3.9 times longer. In a liquid with n_m > n, a convex lens even becomes **diverging**.

*Problem.* A convex lens of f = 20 cm in air (n = 1.5) placed in water: f_water = 20 × 0.5/0.128 ≈ **78 cm**.

check.q: A double-convex lens has R₁ = 10 cm, R₂ = −15 cm and n = 1.5. Its focal length is:

sections.md:
*Convex lens, real image.* f = +15 cm, object at u = −25 cm: 1/v = 1/15 − 1/25 = (5 − 3)/75 = 2/75 ⇒ **v = +37.5 cm**; m = v/u = **−1.5** (real, inverted, enlarged) — a projector.

*Convex lens, magnifier.* f = +10 cm, u = −8 cm: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/8 = −1/40 ⇒ v = −40 cm, m = **+5** (virtual, erect).

*Concave lens.* f = −15 cm, u = −30 cm: 1/v = −1/15 − 1/30 = −3/30 = −1/10 ⇒ v = −10 cm; m = +1/3 — always virtual, erect, diminished.

**Thin lenses in contact:** **1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂**, **P = P₁ + P₂**; total magnification m = m₁m₂.

*Problem.* Lenses of +10 cm and −15 cm in contact: P = 10 − 6.67 = +3.33 D ⇒ f = **+30 cm** (converging). Spectacle makers combine lenses this way, and camera lenses use combinations to reduce defects (aberrations).

*Power.* A lens of −2.5 D has f = −40 cm, a concave lens — used for myopia.

**Displacement method.** For a fixed object–screen distance D > 4f, a convex lens gives a sharp image at two positions a distance d apart: **f = (D² − d²)/(4D)**. With D = 90 cm and d = 20 cm: f = (8100 − 400)/360 ≈ **21.4 cm**.

check.q: Lenses of power +5 D and −3 D are in contact. The focal length of the combination is:
check.why: P = 5 − 3 = +2 D, so f = 1/2 m = 50 cm, converging.

sections.md:
For a prism of angle A: **r₁ + r₂ = A** and the deviation **δ = i + e − A**. As i increases, δ first falls and then rises; at **minimum deviation** δ_m, i = e and r₁ = r₂ = A/2, so

**n = sin((A + δ_m)/2)/sin(A/2)**.

*Problem.* A 60° prism gives δ_m = 30° for a certain light: n = sin 45°/sin 30° = 0.707/0.5 ≈ **1.414**.

*Problem.* The same prism immersed in water (n = 1.33): relative index 1.414/1.33 ≈ 1.063, so sin((60° + δ′)/2) = 1.063 × 0.5 = 0.532 ⇒ (60° + δ′)/2 ≈ 32.1° ⇒ δ′ ≈ **4.2°** — much less bending.

**Thin prism:** for small A, δ = (n − 1)A.

**Dispersion.** n is larger for violet than for red, so violet deviates more and white light spreads into a spectrum. **Rainbows** form when sunlight is refracted, dispersed and internally reflected in raindrops; the primary bow appears at about 42° from the anti-solar point, red on the outside. **Blue sky** comes from scattering (strongest for short wavelengths), and **red sunsets** happen because the blue has been scattered out of the long path through the air.

check.q: At minimum deviation in a prism of angle A:
check.why: The ray passes symmetrically, so the two internal angles are equal and add to A.

sections.h: The eye, the microscope and the telescope
sections.md:
**The eye.** A convex lens system focuses images on the retina; ciliary muscles change the lens's focal length (**accommodation**). Near point D ≈ 25 cm, far point at infinity.
- **Myopia** (short sight): image forms in front of the retina — corrected with a **concave** lens of f = −(far point). A person who sees clearly only up to 80 cm needs f = −80 cm, P = −1.25 D.
- **Hypermetropia** (long sight): near point is farther than 25 cm — corrected with a **convex** lens.
- **Presbyopia**: loss of accommodation with age — bifocals.
- **Astigmatism**: cornea not spherical — cylindrical lenses.

**Simple microscope (magnifier).** m = 1 + D/f (image at near point) or D/f (image at infinity, relaxed eye). For f = 5 cm: m = 6 or 5.

**Compound microscope.** Objective (short f_o) gives a real magnified image; eyepiece magnifies it further. With image at infinity, **m ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e)**, L = tube length.
*Problem.* f_o = 2.0 cm, f_e = 6.25 cm, image at near point (25 cm). Eyepiece: v_e = −25 cm ⇒ 1/u_e = 1/v_e − 1/f_e = −1/25 − 1/6.25 = −5/25 ⇒ u_e = −5 cm. If the objective's image must be 5 cm from the eyepiece and the lenses are 15 cm apart, then v_o = 10 cm; 1/u_o = 1/10 − 1/2 = −4/10 ⇒ u_o = −2.5 cm. m = (v_o/u_o)(1 + D/f_e) = (−4)(5) = **−20**.

**Astronomical telescope.** Objective of large f_o, eyepiece of small f_e. Normal adjustment (final image at infinity): **m = f_o/f_e**, tube length f_o + f_e.
*Problem.* f_o = 140 cm, f_e = 5 cm ⇒ m = **28**, length 145 cm.

**Reflecting telescopes** use a concave mirror as objective: no chromatic aberration, a parabolic mirror removes spherical aberration, and mirrors can be made far larger and lighter than lenses (supported from behind). India's 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope near Nainital is a reflector. A large aperture collects more light and resolves finer detail.

check.q: An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has f_o = 140 cm and f_e = 5 cm. Its magnifying power is:
check.why: m = f_o/f_e = 140/5 = 28; the tube length is f_o + f_e = 145 cm.

workedExamples.q: Object 27 cm from a concave mirror of R = 36 cm. Find the image.
workedExamples.answer: Real, inverted, 54 cm in front, twice the size

workedExamples.q: A convex lens of f = 15 cm with an object at 25 cm. Find v and m.
Focal length of a double-convex lens, R₁ = 10 cm, R₂ = −15 cm, n = 1.5.
A 60° prism has δ_m = 30°. Find n.
A myopic person's far point is 80 cm. What lens is needed?
steps: Lens must image infinity at −80 cm: f = −80 cm.

workedExamples.q: Magnifying power of a telescope with f_o = 140 cm, f_e = 5 cm in normal adjustment.

summary: Use the Cartesian sign convention: distances along incident light positive.
Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, m = −v/u; lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u.
Concave mirror and convex lens can form real images; convex mirror and concave lens only virtual, diminished ones.
Apparent depth = real depth/n; slab shift = t(1 − 1/n).
TIR: sin C = 1/n; used in fibres, prisms, diamonds; explains mirages.
Spherical surface: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R.
Lens-maker: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂); in a liquid use n/n_m.
Lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂.
Prism: n = sin((A + δ_m)/2)/sin(A/2); thin prism δ = (n − 1)A.
Violet deviates most; rainbows, blue sky and red sunsets come from dispersion and scattering.
Myopia → concave lens; hypermetropia → convex lens.
Microscope m ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e); telescope m = f_o/f_e.
Reflecting telescopes avoid chromatic aberration and can be very large.

rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch10-wave-optics.title: Wave Optics
rd-school-c12-physics-b.ch10-wave-optics.subtitle: How light plus light can make darkness — and why your sunglasses cut glare

sections.md:
Tilt a CD under a tube light and it flashes with rainbow colours, though it has no pigment. Look at a soap bubble or a film of petrol on a wet road after monsoon rain: shimmering coloured bands. Ray optics, which treats light as straight lines, cannot explain these. They need **wave optics**.

In 1637 Descartes gave a corpuscular picture of light, and Newton developed it: light as a stream of tiny particles (corpuscles). In 1678 the Dutch physicist **Christiaan Huygens** put forward the **wave theory**. Both models could explain reflection and refraction, but they made opposite predictions about the speed of light in a denser medium:

| Model | Prediction for speed in water |
|---|---|
| Corpuscular (Newton) | faster than in air |
| Wave (Huygens) | slower than in air |

The wave model was not accepted at first, partly because of Newton's authority and partly because light seemed to travel in perfectly straight lines (we now know this is because its wavelength is tiny, about 0.4–0.7 μm, compared to everyday objects). In 1801 **Thomas Young** performed his double-slit interference experiment, which firmly supported waves. In 1850 Foucault measured the speed of light in water and found it **less** than in air. Around 1864 **Maxwell** showed that light is an electromagnetic wave, which needs no medium. Later (Chapter 11) we will see that light also shows particle behaviour (photons) — so nature needs both pictures.

This chapter: Huygens' principle → reflection and refraction using wavefronts → coherent and incoherent addition → Young's double-slit interference → single-slit diffraction → validity of ray optics → polarisation.
keyTerms: Corpuscular model — light as particles
Wave model — light as a wave spreading from a source

check.q: Which measurement went against Newton's corpuscular model?
options: Speed of light in water is less than in air
check.why: The corpuscular model predicted light would be faster in water; Foucault found it slower, as the wave model predicted.

sections.md:
Drop a stone in a still pond: circular ripples spread out. Every point on one ripple crest is in the same phase. A **wavefront** is the locus (surface) of all points vibrating in the **same phase**. The speed with which a wavefront moves outward is the wave speed, and the energy travels **perpendicular** to the wavefront — that perpendicular direction is what we call a **ray**.

- A **point source** gives **spherical** wavefronts; intensity falls as 1/r².
- A **line source** (like a long slit) gives **cylindrical** wavefronts.
- At a very large distance, a small portion of a sphere is nearly flat: a **plane wavefront** (sunlight on Earth).

**Huygens' principle** lets us find the shape of the wavefront at a later time if we know it now:
1. Every point on a wavefront is a source of **secondary wavelets**, which spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave.
2. The new wavefront after time t is the **common tangent (forward envelope)** of these wavelets, each of radius vt.

Huygens also had to explain why there is no wave travelling backwards. He simply assumed the amplitude of secondary wavelets is maximum forward and zero backward. This *ad hoc* assumption was later justified by more rigorous wave theory.

Think of a line of students at assembly who each take one step forward: the new line is where all their feet land.

keyTerms: Wavefront — surface of constant phase
Secondary wavelet — tiny spherical wave from each point on a wavefront
Envelope — common tangent to all wavelets

check.q: The wavefronts of sunlight reaching Earth are approximately:
check.why: At a huge distance from the Sun, a small piece of a giant sphere is practically flat, i.e. a plane wavefront.

sections.h: 3. Refraction and reflection of plane waves using Huygens' principle
sections.md:
**Refraction (denser medium, v₂ < v₁).** A plane wavefront AB meets the surface PP′ at angle i. Let τ be the time taken by the wavefront to travel BC = v₁τ in medium 1. In that same time, the wavelet from A travels AE = v₂τ in medium 2. Draw a tangent CE from C to the sphere of radius v₂τ about A: CE is the refracted wavefront at angle r.

From triangles ABC and AEC:
- sin i = BC/AC = v₁τ/AC
- sin r = AE/AC = v₂τ/AC

So **sin i / sin r = v₁/v₂**. With refractive index n = c/v, this gives **n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r** — **Snell's law**! Since v₂ < v₁, r < i: the ray bends towards the normal.

If λ₁, λ₂ are wavelengths in the two media, the frequency stays the same (it is fixed by the source), so v₁/v₂ = λ₁/λ₂. Light becomes **shorter-wavelength** in a denser medium, but its **frequency does not change**.

**Refraction at a rarer medium (v₂ > v₁).** The same construction gives r > i: bending away from the normal. When i equals the **critical angle** i_c, with sin i_c = n₂/n₁, r becomes 90°. For i > i_c no refracted wave exists: **total internal reflection**.

**Reflection.** Wavefront AB hits a mirror at angle i. In time τ, B moves to C (BC = vτ); the wavelet from A, in the same medium, has radius AE = vτ. The tangent CE is the reflected wavefront. Triangles EAC and BAC are congruent, so **i = r** — the law of reflection.

**What happens to a wavefront after optical devices?**
- Plane wave through a thin **prism**: the part through the thick base is slowed more, so the wavefront tilts — the beam deviates towards the base.
- Plane wave through a **convex lens**: the centre (thickest) is delayed most, so the emerging wavefront is spherical and converges to the focus.
- Plane wave on a **concave mirror**: the reflected wavefront is spherical, converging to the focus.

An important insight: the time taken from a point on the object to the corresponding point on the image is the **same along every ray**. That is why a lens gives a sharp image — all rays arrive in phase.

**The Doppler effect for light.** If a source moves away from us, the received frequency decreases (wavelength increases): **red shift**. If it moves towards us: **blue shift**. For speeds much less than c, Δν/ν = −v_radial/c. Astronomers use red shifts of galaxies to measure how fast they recede — this is how the expansion of the universe was discovered.

check.q: When light goes from air into glass, which quantity stays the same?
check.why: Frequency is set by the source, so it is unchanged; speed and wavelength both decrease in glass.

sections.h: 4. Coherent and incoherent addition of waves
sections.md:
Two needles dipped up and down together in a water tray create two sets of ripples. Where crest meets crest, the water heaves hard; where crest meets trough, it is calm. This is **interference**, based on the **superposition principle**: the resultant displacement is the vector sum of individual displacements.

Let two sources S₁ and S₂ vibrate in phase, each giving displacement y = a cos ωt at a point P.
- If the **path difference** S₁P − S₂P = nλ (n = 0, 1, 2…), the waves arrive in phase: amplitude 2a, intensity **4I₀**. **Constructive interference**.
- If the path difference = (n + ½)λ, they arrive in opposite phase: amplitude zero, intensity **0**. **Destructive interference**.

In general, if the phase difference is φ, the resultant intensity is

**I = 4 I₀ cos²(φ/2)**

(for two equal waves each of intensity I₀). Phase difference and path difference are related by φ = (2π/λ) × path difference.

**Coherent sources** keep a **constant phase difference** with time. Then the pattern of bright and dark spots is steady and visible. **Incoherent sources** have a phase difference that changes rapidly and randomly. Then cos²(φ/2) averages to ½ and I = 2I₀ everywhere — just the sum of intensities, no pattern. Two separate bulbs are incoherent because each atom emits light randomly for about 10⁻⁸ s at a time. So to see interference with light, we must derive both sources **from a single source** — Young's trick.

Note: energy is not destroyed in interference. It is only **redistributed** — what is missing at dark fringes appears at bright ones (average intensity stays 2I₀).
keyTerms: Superposition — displacements add
Coherent — constant phase difference
Path difference — difference in distances from the two sources

check.q: Two coherent waves of intensity I₀ each meet with phase difference π/2. The resultant intensity is:
check.why: I = 4I₀cos²(π/4) = 4I₀ × ½ = 2I₀.

sections.h: 5. Interference of light waves: Young's double-slit experiment
sections.md:
In 1801 Young made two pinholes (later slits) S₁ and S₂ close together on an opaque screen and lit them with light from a single pinhole S. Because S₁ and S₂ were fed by the same wavefront, they behaved as **coherent sources**. On a distant screen he saw **alternate bright and dark bands — fringes**.

**Fringe positions.** Let slit separation be d, screen distance D (D ≫ d), and P a point at height x from the centre O. Then

path difference S₂P − S₁P ≈ x d / D

- **Bright fringe:** x d/D = nλ ⟹ **xₙ = nλD/d**
- **Dark fringe:** x d/D = (n + ½)λ ⟹ **xₙ = (n + ½)λD/d**

**Fringe width** (distance between consecutive bright or dark fringes):

**β = λD/d**

All fringes are equally spaced. The central point O (path difference zero) is always **bright**. Angular fringe width θ = λ/d.

**What changes the pattern?**
- Bigger D or bigger λ → wider fringes; bigger d → narrower fringes.
- Red light gives wider fringes than blue (λ larger).
- **White light:** the central fringe is white (all colours have zero path difference there). On either side, the fringes are coloured — the blue edge closer to the centre, red farther — and after a few fringes colours overlap and the screen looks uniformly whitish.
- Immerse the apparatus in water (n = 1.33): λ becomes λ/n, so fringes shrink.
- If the source slit S is too wide, or S₁S₂ is not lit coherently, fringes blur. For good fringes the condition s/S < λ/d (s = source size, S = distance from source to slits) should hold.
- Moving the source S slightly up shifts the whole pattern down (the centre moves to where the total path difference is zero).

This experiment gave the first measurement of the wavelength of light — and the first strong proof of its wave nature.

fig.caption: Young's experiment: two coherent slits send overlapping waves; the screen shows equally spaced bright and dark fringes.
fig.alt: Two slits emitting circular waves onto a screen with red and black fringes

check.q: In YDSE, if the slit separation d is doubled and D is halved, the fringe width becomes:
check.why: β = λD/d, so halving D and doubling d makes β one-fourth of its value.

sections.md:
Look at a distant street light through the narrow gap between two fingers, or at a tube light through a fine cloth: you see fuzzy bands. Light **bends around obstacles and spreads after passing through small openings** — this is **diffraction**. It is noticeable only when the opening is comparable to the wavelength. Sound (λ ≈ 1 m) diffracts around doors easily, which is why you can hear around corners but not see around them.

**Single slit of width a**, lit by a plane wave, observed far away (or at the focal plane of a lens).
- At the centre, all secondary wavelets from the slit arrive in phase: a broad, bright **central maximum**.
- At angle θ where **a sin θ = nλ** (n = ±1, ±2…), intensity is **zero** (minima). Reason: divide the slit into two halves; for every point in the top half there is a point in the bottom half whose wavelet is exactly λ/2 out of step, so they cancel in pairs. For n = 2, split into four parts, and so on.
- Secondary maxima occur roughly at **a sin θ ≈ (n + ½)λ**, getting weaker: only part of the slit is uncancelled (one-third at n = 1, so much dimmer).

Angular width of the central maximum = **2λ/a**; its linear width on a screen at distance D = **2λD/a**. A narrower slit gives a **wider** central maximum.

**Interference vs diffraction**

| Interference (YDSE) | Diffraction (single slit) |
|---|---|
| Superposition of two waves from two sources | Superposition of a continuous family of wavelets from one wavefront |
| Fringes equally wide | Central maximum twice as wide as others |
| All bright fringes nearly equally bright | Intensity falls rapidly away from centre |
| Maxima at path difference nλ | Minima at a sin θ = nλ |

In a real double-slit experiment, each slit also diffracts: the interference fringes appear inside a broad single-slit diffraction envelope.

**Seeing it yourself.** Hold two razor blades edge to edge to make a narrow slit and look at a line filament bulb through it. You will see a bright central band flanked by fainter bands; coloured if the light is white.

check.why: Its angular width is 2λ/a, so smaller a means a wider central maximum.

sections.h: 7. Validity of ray optics: the Fresnel distance
sections.md:
If diffraction spreads every beam, why does ray optics work so well for lenses and mirrors? Consider a beam passing through an aperture of size a. Diffraction spreads it by an angle about λ/a. After travelling a distance z, the spread is about zλ/a. This spreading becomes comparable to the aperture itself when

zλ/a ≈ a ⟹ **z_F = a²/λ** (the **Fresnel distance**)

For distances much less than z_F, the beam's spreading is negligible and **ray optics is valid**. For distances beyond z_F, diffraction dominates.

Example: a = 3 mm, λ = 500 nm gives z_F = (3×10⁻³)² / (5×10⁻⁷) = 9×10⁻⁶ / 5×10⁻⁷ = **18 m**. So in a school lab, light through a 3 mm hole behaves like rays. Ray optics is the limit of wave optics when λ → 0.

**Did you know?** Diffraction also limits how sharply a telescope or microscope can see (its resolving power). Bigger telescope mirrors see finer detail partly for this reason.

check.q: The Fresnel distance for an aperture a and wavelength λ is:
check.why: Spreading zλ/a equals a when z = a²/λ.

sections.md:
Tie one end of a long rope to a wall and shake the other up and down: a transverse wave runs along with the rope moving vertically — a **plane (linearly) polarised** wave. Shake it in all directions randomly and you get an **unpolarised** wave. Now pass the rope through a vertical slit in a board: only the vertical vibrations pass. A horizontal slit after it would block everything.

Light is a transverse EM wave; its electric field vibrates perpendicular to the direction of travel. Ordinary light (Sun, bulb) is **unpolarised**: the E-field direction changes randomly. A **Polaroid** (a sheet with long aligned molecules) acts like the slit: it passes only the component of E along its **pass axis**, so the light coming out is **linearly polarised** and its intensity is **I₀/2** (half) for unpolarised input.

**Malus' law.** If polarised light of intensity I₀ falls on a second Polaroid (the *analyser*) whose axis makes angle θ with the light's polarisation, the transmitted intensity is

**I = I₀ cos²θ**

Rotating the analyser makes the light go bright–dark–bright twice per full turn. Crossed Polaroids (θ = 90°) block all light. Insert a third Polaroid at 45° between crossed Polaroids and some light gets through — a favourite exam puzzle.

**Polarisation by scattering.** Blue sky light, viewed at 90° to the direction of the Sun, is strongly polarised. Electrons in air molecules oscillate with the incoming E-field and re-radiate; at 90°, only oscillations perpendicular to your line of sight can send light to you. Bees and some birds use sky polarisation to navigate.

**Polarisation by reflection — Brewster's law.** When unpolarised light reflects from glass or water, the reflected light is partly polarised. At one special angle — the **Brewster angle** i_B — the reflected light is **completely polarised** (perpendicular to the plane of incidence) and the reflected and refracted rays are **at 90°** to each other. Then

**tan i_B = n** (refractive index of the reflecting medium relative to the incident one)

For glass, n = 1.5 gives i_B ≈ 56.3°; for water, n = 1.33 gives about 53°.

**Uses:** polarising sunglasses cut glare from roads and water (reflected light is mostly horizontally polarised); Polaroid filters in cameras; LCD screens of calculators and phones; 3D movie glasses; studying stress in plastics.

rd-corporate-emails-people-read.title: Writing Emails People Actually Read
rd-corporate-emails-people-read.subtitle: Subject lines, the first two sentences, and the art of the clear ask

sections.md:
Imagine a regional sales head in Mumbai opening her laptop at 8:30 a.m. She has 143 unread emails. She will not read them all. She will scan subject lines and the first line or two of each, decide in a few seconds whether to open, defer, or archive — and move on. Your carefully written three-paragraph email about the delayed vendor invoice is competing with 142 others.

This is the reality of workplace email: **your reader is busy, distracted and reading on a phone**. Writing for that reader is not about fancy vocabulary. It is about making three things obvious within seconds:

1. **What is this about?** (subject line)
2. **What do you need from me, and by when?** (first two sentences)
3. **What do I need to know to do it?** (the rest, short and scannable)

If you get these right, people reply faster, meetings disappear, and you gain a reputation as someone who is *easy to work with* — one of the most valuable reputations in any office.

> **Did you know?** Journalists call the practice of putting the most important information first the *inverted pyramid*. Business writers borrowed it, and the military uses a similar idea called **BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front**.
